#767. AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab."

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes

For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back."

The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man

An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation."

The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person

A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around."

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight

The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration."

The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

Materials provided by University of California - Santa Barbara. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#766. Patrick Stewart’s Cause of Death Revealed After Water Cremation

Less than a month after Patrick Stewart died at the age of 86, his official cause of death was confirmed to be Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to his death certificate.

More details about Patrick Stewart’s death have come to light.

Less than a month after the X-Men actor died at the age of 86, his official cause of death was determined to be Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to his death certificate obtained by TMZ.

It also listed cardiopulmonary arrest—also known as cardiac arrest—as well as a neurocognitive disorder with Lewy body dementia, which is “a brain disorder that can lead to problems with thinking, movement, behavior, and mood,” per Alzheimers.gov.

The Star Trek: The Next Generation alum’s death certificate stated that his remains underwent alkaline hydrolysis—also known as water cremation—which according to the Cremation Association of North America “uses water, alkaline chemicals, heat, and sometimes pressure and agitation, to accelerate natural decomposition.” The process leaves behind bone fragments and a liquid that can then be safely disposed of.

One day after his Oct. 28 death, Stewart’s family shared that he had passed away at his Los Angeles home “in the loving care of his beloved wife" Sunny Ozell.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” the Oct. 29 post on Stewart’s Instagram read. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

“He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role,” the statement continued, “in his art and life.”

In the weeks following his death, Ozell—whom Stewart married in 2013—shared her own heartbreaking tribute to her late husband, writing on Instagram Nov. 11, “We left nothing unsaid. He knew I loved him, and I know he loved me.”

“We shared nearly two decades together, and we filled those years with so much *living*,” the 47-year-old added. “I’ve been overwhelmed by the public response to Patrick’s death, and while I’m not at all surprised that he touched so many, I’m sincerely moved by the outpouring of sadness and loss.”

For a look at more fond remembrances of Stewart, keep reading.

#765. Childish Gambino’s Politically-Charged ‘This Is America’ Joins YouTube’s Billion Views Club

"This Is America' was a politically-charged shot that rung out around the globe, a hit that touches on gun violence, racism and discrimination in America.

Childish Gambino has joined the club. YouTube’s Billion Views Club, that is, for his 2018 hit “This Is America.”

The official music video for the actor and rapper’s global smash is his first to pass the streaming milestone.

“This Is America’ was a politically-charged shot that rung out around the globe, a song that explores gun violence, racism and discrimination in the United States. It was, of course, powered by its confronting, one-take music video, directed by Hiro Murai and starring Gambino.

The recording debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart (via mcDJ/Wolf + Rothstein/RCA), bowing as the most-streamed and top-selling song of the week. It also arrived atop the U.S. Streaming Songs and Digital Song Sales charts, and topped sales and consumption charts around the globe, including Australia. Explore Childish Gambino See latest videos, charts and news

The single was the first and only Hot 100 leader for Donald Glover’s musical alter ego, who took the stage to unveil it as the musical guest on the May 5, 2018 episode of NBC’s Saturday Night Live, which he also hosted. Related Jordan Brunoli, Bassist With Australian Indie Rockers Bugs, Dies at 31 U2 Ride to No. 1 on ARIA Chart With 'Carnaval De Luz' Gracie Abrams' 'Daughter from Hell' Gets Deluxe Treatment: Stream It Now

On the red carpet of the 2018 Met Gala, Glover spoke briefly about the song and its meaning. In a comment dripping with irony, he remarked that, with “This Is America,” he simply wanted to make a song folks could play on the Fourth of July.

He elaborated in a 2023 interview for a GQ cover story, in which he said the idea for the song “started as a joke,” and that its title was “all we had” at the embryonic stage. “It started as a Drake diss, to be honest, as like a funny way of doing it. But then I was like, this s— sounds kind of hard though. So I was like, let me play with it.”

It was no joke with critics and fans. Glover and co-writer Ludwig Goransson went on to win song of the year with “America” at the 61st Annual Grammy Awards, where it became the first rap song to ever win the prestigious “Big Four” category, which recognizes songwriters. “This Is America” went on to snag a total of four Grammys, including record of the year, best music video, and snagged the MTV Video Music Award for best direction.

The song and its video have enjoyed several afterlives through covers, mashups and parodies.

#764. DWTS’ Val Chmerkovskiy Makes Spicy Comment About Jenna Johnson's Exit

Dancing With the Stars pro Val Chmerkovskiy expressed his support for wife Jenna Johnson following their back-to-back eliminations by giving an NSFW shoutout to his “baddie” wife.

Val Chmerkovskiy and Jenna Johnson may not be adding another Mirrorball to their household, but they're still having a ball at home.

A day after Johnson and her partner Harry Shum Jr. were voted off Dancing With the Stars following his and his partner Jenna Dewan’s elimination the week prior, Chmerkovskiy showed his support for his wife with a steamy comment.

“Keep the trophy’s [sic],” the 40-year-old shared on his Instagram Stories Nov. 18 alongside a photo of Johnson from a red carpet event. “I get to watch this baddie brush her teeth naked every morning.” Chmerkovskiy—who shares son Rome, 3, with his wife of seven years—also thirsted after her by adding a drool emoji.

Johnson and Shum were shockingly sent home on the Nov. 17 semifinals after receiving perfect scores 30 out of 30 for both of their dances: a paso doble to Rihanna's "We Found Love” and a quickstep to Amy Winehouse's “Valerie,” in which Shum paid tribute to late Glee costar Naya Rivera.

While some believe viewers made a major misstep by sending the pair home, the duo slammed the negativity they said they received online, sharing they think it impacted their relationship with the rest of the season 35 cast.

“I hope to get to know them more,” Shum told E! News in an interview following their elimination Nov. 17, “because it's just been so chaotic.”

“We're a bit all trauma bonded,” Johnson chimed in, to which Shum added, “There's a lot of trauma bond just because this year has been a little crazy.”

“Social media is a little nuts,” he continued. “I hope they address that at a certain point, because I think there's a good amount of bullying that doesn't feel really good, and I think the rest of the cast feels it.”

Though Shum didn’t go into specifics, he and Johnson were spun into drama after Chmerkovskiy received a one-week suspension from the show following his now-infamous reaction to a critique judge Carrie Ann Inaba made after one of Johnson and Shum’s performances, in which he referenced Will Smith’s 2022 Oscar slap.

Shum seemingly referred to the fallout as he praised Johnson after they were voted off.

“I want to say you have been dealing with everything with grace, with the noise outside,” the Grey’s Anatomy star told his partner on air, “and teaching me the things that I have only dreamed of to learn, and this has been one of the most beautiful experiences. So, thank you so much.”

As DWTS prepares to tango into its season 35 finale, read on for a deep dive into the secrets of the ballroom…

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones said he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last."

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show."

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody."

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together."

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay said on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'"

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna said on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner."

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

"It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well."

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again."

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers."

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee said pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and new in something different every week, so it stays interesting."

#763. A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets

A butterfly commonly seen throughout Central and South America has been concealing a remarkable secret. For more than two centuries, scientists believed that the genus Colobura contained just one widespread species. Now, researchers have identified a third species that looks almost identical to its relatives, raising new questions about how these butterflies evolved and continue to live alongside one another.

The newly identified species, named Colobura cryptica, was described in the journal Zootaxa by researchers led by Anisha Sapkota, a doctoral student at the Florida Museum of Natural History. By combining DNA analysis with subtle differences in wing patterns and ultraviolet light reflection, the team uncovered distinctions that had remained largely invisible to scientists.

Even more surprising, the three species occupy overlapping regions and can be found in the same places at the same time. Yet genetic evidence suggests they remain separate, with no detectable signs of interbreeding.

A Familiar Butterfly With a Hidden Identity

Central and South America's tropical rainforests contain some of the greatest concentrations of biodiversity on the planet. Costa Rica alone supports approximately half a million species, roughly five times the number found across Canada, even though Canada's land area is about 200 times larger.

Despite this extraordinary diversity, certain plants and animals are especially recognizable throughout the region. In Canada's boreal forests, balsam firs are a familiar feature of the landscape. In tropical America, trees belonging to the genus Cecropia play a similarly prominent role.

In 1888, German botanist Andreas Schimper described their importance, writing, "Every naturalist who has been in tropical America will remember Cecropia, belonging to the most conspicuous trees of those countries."

The butterflies of the genus Colobura are just as recognizable, according to Sapkota.

"If you go to the neotropics, Colobura is one of the first butterflies you see," she said.

These butterflies and Cecropia trees share a close ecological relationship because Cecropia leaves provide food for Colobura caterpillars. Both groups occur across an enormous geographic area, from portions of the Andes Mountains and the Brazilian Amazon to the Atlantic Rainforest in Brazil and Paraguay. They are also widespread throughout Central America and the Caribbean Islands.

Such broad distributions are not particularly unusual in tropical ecosystems. However, the diversity within these groups presents an interesting contrast.

Scientists recognize 61 species of Cecropia, many of which occupy relatively small geographic areas. Some grow only in the Andes, while others are confined to the Caribbean.

For Colobura butterflies, the situation appeared very different. After Carl Linnaeus formally described Colobura dirce in 1758, scientists spent more than 200 years treating the genus as a single species, despite its extensive range.

That understanding began to change in 2001, when researchers formally recognized a second species. Now, an unexpected discovery in Venezuela has led to the identification of a third, described by Sapkota and her colleagues in Zootaxa.

Rather than providing a simple explanation for the group's evolutionary history, the discovery has introduced an even greater puzzle.

"It's crazy to think about. These butterflies look almost exactly the same and are found in the exact same place at the same time."

A Butterfly Mystery Dating Back More Than 150 Years

Distinguishing adult Colobura butterflies is exceptionally difficult. Their wings are nearly identical, with only slight variations in a gray stripe on the underside of the front wings. In some butterflies, this stripe becomes a little wider. In others, it stays the same width. It may also extend far enough to meet a yellow band running across the wing, or stop short of it.

Their caterpillars offer somewhat clearer clues.

Colobura caterpillars have velvety black bodies covered with prominent yellow projections that end in sharply angled barbs. These defensive structures send a warning to potential predators that could be interpreted as "leave me alone, or there will be unpleasant consequences."

Beneath those conspicuous spines are much smaller cream-colored markings. Depending on the species, these markings may resemble teardrops or rings, or they may be missing entirely.

The importance of these differences was recognized surprisingly early.

In 1852, Dutch entomologist Jan Sepp proposed that caterpillars with different cream-colored patterns represented two separate species. Other researchers rejected his interpretation, arguing that the variations could reflect differences between males and females or simply natural variation within a single species.

That view remained dominant for approximately 150 years.

In 2001, Keith Willmott and several colleagues revisited Sepp's observations and formally described a second species, Colobura annulata. Willmott is now a curator at the Florida Museum's McGuire Center for Lepidoptera and Biodiversity.

"We assumed that was the problem solved," Willmott said.

He moved on to other research, believing the longstanding classification problem had been resolved. However, occasional observations continued to suggest that something was missing.

"I had a few indications that there was a third species, but I thought it was too implausible."

At the time, even the existence of two nearly indistinguishable species seemed remarkable.

"It's a very distinctive butterfly. It's hard to imagine there being two species in the same area that look alike because they're so different from anything else."

Roughly 25 years later, fresh evidence emerged when Willmott's colleague Andrés Orellana encountered a group of hungry Colobura caterpillars feeding on a young Cecropia tree in Venezuela.

The caterpillars were rapidly stripping leaves from the sapling. They possessed the familiar black body segments near the head and yellow spines characteristic of the genus, but one feature stood out.

Unlike the two recognized species, these caterpillars had no cream-colored markings at all.

Orellana photographed the unusual insects and shared the images with Willmott. The discovery provided a compelling reason to investigate whether a third species had been overlooked.

Sapkota had recently joined the Shirey lab at the Florida Museum and was eager to lead the investigation.

Working with her colleagues, she designed a study that combined genetic evidence with careful examinations of butterfly anatomy.

First, she studied DNA barcodes, short and highly variable genetic sequences that help researchers distinguish species. These sequences came from a long-running survey of butterflies and moths in Costa Rica led by study co-authors Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs.

The investigation then expanded to older butterfly specimens collected across tropical Central and South America. Sapkota sent these museum samples to Nick Grishin at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, where researchers sequenced both their mitochondrial and nuclear genomes.

The genetic results provided a way to test whether the butterflies represented genuinely different evolutionary groups rather than ordinary variations within a single species.

But the researchers also wanted to know whether there were physical differences that previous scientists had failed to notice.

An Invisible Clue Hidden in Butterfly Wings

Sapkota spent hours examining preserved butterflies in museum collections, searching for consistent traits that might distinguish the suspected species.

At first, the effort produced few answers. Other than the slight differences in the gray wing stripe, the butterflies appeared remarkably similar.

Eventually, she noticed something unusual.

The undersides of some wings appeared to have a faint violet shimmer, and the intensity of that sheen seemed to vary between specimens.

This observation suggested that the insects might reflect ultraviolet light, which falls outside the range of human vision but can be detected by many butterflies.

"I checked it with a spectrometer and found that even though the butterflies didn't look violet to me, it reflected UV light," she said.

The measurements revealed a striking pattern. All three species reflected ultraviolet light, but the wavelengths differed.

The researchers named the newly identified species Colobura cryptica, reflecting its previously concealed identity.

Although the visible differences were extremely subtle, the ultraviolet measurements, caterpillar markings, and DNA results told a consistent story.

The three species could be distinguished by the following features:

There is an additional complication with Colobura dirce. It includes two subspecies with different ultraviolet reflectance values. Colobura dirce dirce reflects light at 362.2 nm, while Colobura dirce wolcotti reflects light at 390.6 nm. The 376 nm value represents the average for the species.

Beyond these minor wing differences, Sapkota could not identify any other consistent anatomical distinctions. Even the male genitalia, which often provide some of the most reliable features for separating butterfly and moth species, appeared indistinguishable.

Nevertheless, the genetic findings were decisive.

DNA analysis identified three distinct evolutionary lineages, and those divisions matched the physical differences the team had documented. Together, the evidence confirmed that Colobura contains three species rather than two.

Three Butterfly Species Living Side by Side

Identifying a previously unknown butterfly species is significant on its own, but the geographic distributions of these three species make the finding particularly intriguing.

All three occur in overlapping portions of Central and South America.

Colobura dirce has the widest distribution, extending from Mexico to southeastern Brazil. It occurs on both sides of the Andes Mountains and throughout the Caribbean archipelago.

Colobura annulata also occupies a large geographic area, although it is absent from the Greater Antilles.

The newly described Colobura cryptica has the smallest known range, stretching from southern Mexico to the foothills of the Andes.

These overlapping distributions raise an important evolutionary question. How did three species become genetically distinct while continuing to occupy many of the same regions?

Species often emerge when populations become isolated from one another. A mountain range, for example, might divide a population and prevent individuals on opposite sides from mating.

Over many generations, the separated groups can accumulate different genetic and physical traits. If those differences become great enough, the populations may eventually lose the ability to interbreed, even if they come into contact again.

But geographic separation is not the only mechanism that can drive the formation of new species.

Researchers suspect that the Colobura butterflies might have developed different ways of using their shared forest habitats.

"There could be vertical stratification between these butterflies," Sapkota said. "Colobura dirce is typically found in the undergrowth and C. cryptica and C. annulata are usually found in the canopy, but we do not know for sure because there have been mixed signals coming from different studies."

In other words, one species may spend more time near the forest floor while the others favor the upper branches.

This kind of habitat separation could potentially help maintain differences between species living in the same geographic area.

However, previous research has produced inconsistent observations. One reason may be that even experienced butterfly specialists have difficulty telling the three species apart.

How Do Nearly Identical Butterflies Recognize Each Other?

An even more puzzling question concerns how the butterflies identify suitable mates.

Many moths and some butterflies use special scent glands to release pheromones, chemical signals that help individuals recognize members of their own species.

That suggests visual information may play an important role in mate selection. Yet their nearly identical appearance makes it difficult to understand how they distinguish one species from another.

The newly discovered ultraviolet differences offer a possible explanation.

Although humans cannot see ultraviolet light, many butterflies can. Sapkota suspects that the different ultraviolet reflections from their wings might provide visual signals that help them identify members of their own species.

Similar mechanisms are known or suspected in other butterflies and moths. Garden whites, sulfur butterflies, and wood tiger moths possess ultraviolet-reflecting wing scales that researchers believe may contribute to mate selection.

Sapkota is investigating whether Colobura butterflies use comparable signals, but the results have not yet provided a clear answer.

Whatever mechanism they use, the butterflies appear remarkably successful at maintaining their separate identities.

Analysis of nuclear DNA found no evidence of hybridization among the three species, despite their overlapping ranges.

The findings suggest that the species have followed separate evolutionary paths without detectable genetic mixing.

A Familiar Butterfly Still Holds Many Secrets

The discovery of Colobura cryptica demonstrates how much remains unknown about even widespread, conspicuous animals.

For generations, naturalists studied these butterflies without recognizing the full diversity hidden within the group. Only by combining detailed observations with modern genetic testing and ultraviolet measurements were researchers able to uncover the third species.

Yet some of the most important questions remain unanswered, including how the butterflies choose mates, whether they occupy different parts of the forest, and what originally caused their evolutionary separation.

For Sapkota, answering those questions will require observing the insects in their natural habitats.

"Someone has to go the field to find it out themselves."

Those interested in another unusual aspect of Colobura biology can explore the Biodiversity Heritage Library, which contains a whimsical account published in 1952 describing the poop perches that young Colobura caterpillars construct during their earliest developmental stages.

Additional study co-authors include Andrés Orellana of the Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira; Nick Grishin and Leina Song of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center; Isidro Chacón of the Museo Nacional Santo Domingo de Heredia; Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs of the University of Pennsylvania; and Sajan KC of the Florida Museum of Natural History.

The research received partial funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Welch Foundation, Canada's New Frontiers in Research Fund (NFRFt-2020- 00073), the Canada Foundation for Innovation's Major Science Infrastructure program (MSI 42450), BioAlfa, and Project UNET (Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira).

A little piece of Dolly Parton was at the 2026 CMA Awards.

Nearly two months after the country music legend died, her niece Danielle Parton—who was named the brand ambassador of Dolly’s estate last month—wore a dress custom-made for the “Jolene” singer.

“It was made for the ‘Light of Clear Blue Morning’ video that she never got to finish and get to do,” Danielle told E! News in an exclusive interview on the red carpet. “So I'm wearing it tonight in honor of her.”

And while Dolly’s niece may have been inspired by the “I Will Always Love You” singer’s wardrobe, she quickly found that her aunt Dolly’s words of wisdom have left a far greater impact.

“Almost immediately right after she passed, I gave myself one day to sit around and cry and feel pitiful about it,” Danielle continued. “Then the following day I had stuff to do, and I remember she'd always say, ‘Well, you just got to get your rear in gear and get to it.’ So that's what I did.”

But Danielle knows that Dolly’s impact goes far beyond the Parton family.

#759. Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?

Should young people in Germany be more worried about their future than Baby Boomers were in the 1980s and 1990s? Or should both generations take to the streets and protest together? DW checked the data.

Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.

But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today."

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?"

His straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.

The facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.

By 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

There are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.

This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), in 2025, an average of 11% of the population spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing costs. Among people at risk of poverty, the figure was as high as 35%.

However, according to calculations by real estate platform Jacasa, Boomers could actually help ease pressure on the housing market in the coming years. They currently own around 4.8 million owner-occupied houses and apartments.

Over the coming decades, these properties are expected to change hands as former occupants sell them, move into assisted living, or hand them down through inheritance. In some regions, this could lead to an oversupply of properties and, consequently, lower prices, according to Jacasa's projections.

According to the federal government's Education Finance Report, public spending on education for people under 30 has doubled since 2011, rising from around €4,000 to approximately €8,000 per person annually.

Despite this increase, Germany ranks only in the middle of the pack internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), public education spending accounted for 4.6% of Germany's gross domestic product (GDP) in 2022, compared with an OECD average of 4.7%.

However, the additional funding cannot solve the problem of teacher shortages. According to estimates by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, Germany will be short of around 27,000 teachers by 2035. The main reasons are the wave of Baby Boomer retirements and declining birth rates, which have contributed to a shortage of young teachers.

Back in 1972, the Club of Rome warned of the consequences of global warming in its landmark publication The Limits to Growth. According to the United Nations, the planet is on track for 2.6°C of warming by the end of the century compared with pre-industrial levels.

If the world maintains its current climate policies, children who are six years old today could experience heat waves two to seven times as often as Boomers did over their lifetimes. That was the finding of a 2025 study by Vrije University in Brussels.

The deadly impact of extreme weather is already evident in rising death tolls during recent heatwaves. According to Germany's Robert Koch Institute (RKI), an estimated 16,000 people died from heat-related causes across Germany by mid-September 2026. The vast majority — more than 14,000 — were over the age of 65.

"Gen Z and Baby Boomers are in the same boat. We need to bring them together, because otherwise younger people have no prospects for prosperity, and neither do older generations," youth researcher Schnetzer concludes.

He suggests that both generations take to the streets and protest together, adding that would just be the beginning. "What needs to follow is a constructive process to define goals and measures that everyone can support," he said. "Even if it means making sacrifices."

This article was originally published in German.

#758. Where are all the males? Ancient human fossils reveal a startling mystery

Deep inside South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, scientists have uncovered a surprising clue about an extinct human relative that lived hundreds of thousands of years ago. For the first time, researchers have recovered and studied ancient proteins from Homo naledi fossils, revealing evidence that the cave may have contained an exclusively female burial site.

The discovery, published in the journal Cell, raises an extraordinary possibility. The cave could represent the earliest known burial location reserved for one sex by a human relative other than Homo sapiens.

Homo naledi lived approximately 335,000 to 241,000 years ago and has fascinated scientists since its discovery in 2013. This extinct species combined primitive features resembling those of apes with other characteristics more closely associated with modern humans.

A Strange Mystery Hidden in Ancient Human Fossils

One of the biggest puzzles surrounding Homo naledi involves the remarkably similar appearance of adult fossils recovered from the cave's Dinaledi Chamber. For more than a decade, researchers have struggled to explain why these individuals showed so little of the physical variation normally associated with differences between males and females.

To investigate, an international research team involving the University of York, the University of Copenhagen, and more than 10 other institutions turned to proteins preserved in the ancient remains.

The scientists used a technique involving gentle acid etching to recover tiny protein fragments known as peptides from fossilized tooth enamel. This approach allowed them to collect samples while minimizing damage to the valuable fossils. In total, they examined 23 teeth belonging to at least 20 different individuals.

The researchers specifically searched for Amelogenin-Y, a protein produced from a gene on the male Y chromosome. Surprisingly, they found no evidence of this male-specific marker.

To verify that their findings were reliable, specialists at the University of York's chemistry facility examined the amino acids in the samples. Their analysis confirmed that the proteins were genuinely ancient rather than the result of contamination from modern sources.

Could Homo naledi Have Had an All-Female Burial Site?

Dr. Marc Dickinson, from the University of York's Department of Chemistry, said: "The lack of male markers with the group is truly fascinating. It is incredibly exciting to gain a window not only into the biology of our ancestors, but also into how they lived.

"These findings offer rare insights into a culture that has, until now, been difficult to access directly. Advances in ancient protein analysis are opening the door to a far richer and more nuanced understanding of ancient hominins."

The results raise important questions about how Homo naledi individuals lived, organized their communities, and treated their dead. If the Dinaledi Chamber was intentionally used only for females, it could point to surprisingly elaborate social customs among these ancient human relatives.

Such a practice might even suggest symbolic burial traditions once believed to be exclusive to Homo sapiens, or modern humans.

However, the researchers emphasize that an all-female burial site is not the only possible interpretation of the evidence.

Another explanation involves the genetics of Homo naledi itself. If the population lived in extreme isolation, the gene responsible for producing Amelogenin-Y could have undergone a mutation or disappeared entirely.

Under that scenario, some of the individuals could actually have been male, even though their teeth did not contain the protein normally used to identify them.

Ancient Tooth Enamel Opens a New Window Into Human Evolution

The ability to recover proteins from fossils this old is particularly valuable because tooth enamel can protect biological material for extraordinarily long periods.

Palesa Madupe, who carried out the research during her postdoctoral work at the University of Copenhagen, explained why teeth offer such an important source of evidence.

"Unlike those found in other remains like bone fragments, proteins in tooth enamel are preserved because dental enamel -- the hardest tissue in the human body -- shields proteins from environmental contamination even for millions of years.

"This makes them ideal carriers of genetic information from deep time. Our study helps in the long-standing mystery of why Homo naledi lacked significant variation; it's probably because they could have all belonged to one sex."

The research represents the largest collection of individuals from an extinct hominin species ever examined using ancient protein analysis.

Whether the fossils belong entirely to females or include males with an unusual genetic signature, the discovery provides an important new perspective on Homo naledi. It also demonstrates how proteins preserved in ancient teeth can reveal clues about extinct human relatives that their bones alone cannot provide.

As researchers continue investigating the mystery, the findings could reshape our understanding of the social lives and possible burial traditions of ancient human species.

#757. DWTS' Alfonso Ribeiro Sets Record Straight on Voting Point System

After Dancing With the Stars shockingly eliminated Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson in the semi-finals, host Alfonso Ribeiro chimed in on fan speculation about how the show's ranking system works.

Alfonso Ribeiro has proof that on Dancing With the Stars, the numbers add up.

After a season of nail-biting eliminations, the DWTS host responded to a fan theory stating contestants are ranked twice in numerical order—from highest to lowest—based on their scores from the judges' panel and again from the audience vote. From there, the theory suggests each star is awarded two sets of points to match their numerical positions in each ranking.

But the Fresh Prince of Bel-Air alum shut down the assumption that two stars ranking the same—like when Amber Glenn and Jenna Dewan both earned 30 points from the judges in week nine—would result in skipping the next lowest position altogether, impacting the number of points all lower stars would receive toward escaping elimination.

"Now do the math with no breaks in the scores. It doesn’t skip 5," Ribeiro wrote Nov. 18, referring to how Harry Shum Jr. earning the highest judges' score of the seven contestants ranked him highest at number seven, followed by Glenn and Dewan tying for sixth, while placing Maura Higgins at fifth position instead of fourth. "Maura would get 5. No skip."

And since Ezra Frech, Tatyana Ali and Connor Wood all earned the same lowest score of 27 points that week, Ribeiro again clarified how they would all rank the same, in the next position behind Higgins.

As he explained, "The lowest judges scores might be 4 not 3."

In response to sharing the behind-the-scenes insights, the original poster replied, "Speechless! Ahhh making these adjustments! Thanks Alfonso!"

And it's not the only time the 55-year-old has separated fact from fiction when it comes to the competition series. He also responded to the theory that the show was rigged against certain competitors following Hayes Grier's elimination in season 21.

"No chance," Ribeiro replied to a clip of the LexLos podcast discussing speculation about manipulating the vote. "We want everyone who’s popular to stay on. It’s basic logic."

Read on to learn more about who goes in the ballroom after the cameras go down.

How Much Do the Celebrities Get Paid to Be on Dancing With the Stars?

Citing multiple sources, Variety reported in 2019 that Dancing With the Stars contestants make $125,000 for the rehearsal period and first two weeks of the show. If they progress beyond that point, the outlet continued, they earn more money each week. At the time, sources told the publication stars could earn a maximum of $295,000.

However, Bobby Bones said he made more than this when he won season 27 with Sharna Burgess in 2018.

"That show pays OK," the radio personality said on a Sept. 2025 episode of Jason Tartick's podcast Trading Secrets. "Like, first episode, no money. Second episode, $10,000. I think it's like, $10,000, $10,000, $20,000, $20,000. It ends up being $50,000 an episode if you last."

Also receiving a base salary of around $110,000, Bones continued, "I ended up making close to $400,000 from that show."

ABC has not publicly confirmed any of these figures.

What Do the Pros Get Paid on Dancing With the Stars?

Similarly, little has been shared publicly about how much the pros get paid. But as with the contestants, it seems like the longer they're on the show, the more money they can make.

But even if a pro is eliminated in the first round, they're not leaving the ballroom empty-handed.

"You're guaranteed until a certain amount of weeks," Jenna Johnson said on a June 2025 episode of Kelly Stafford and Hank Winchester's podcast The Morning After. "I think there's different contracts though. I can't speak for everybody."

Do Pros Get Paid More If They Win Dancing With the Stars?

While Johnson—who won season 26 with Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon, as well as season 33 with The Bachelor's Joey Graziadei—says the pros don't get a larger paycheck if they take home what is now called the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, she noted there's still an incentive to make it to the finale (besides bragging rights, of course).

"If you make it all the way to the end, you're getting paid the whole season, which is amazing, and you get a bonus on top of that for making it to the finale," she explained on The Morning After. "If you win, it's not like you win a $1 million and split it with your partner. You're just getting a cute trophy together."

Do the Troupe Members Get Paid as Much as the Pros on Dancing With the Stars?

On a 2022 episode of Trading Secrets, Lindsay Arnold recalled how her salary was cut "more than in half" when she was demoted from pro to troupe member.

How Are Pros and Celebrities Paired Together on Dancing With the Stars?

The pros get little input when it comes to being matched with a celebrity.

"You get no say," Lindsay said on a May 2025 episode of Maggie Sellers' Hot Smart Rich podcast. "It's very much just, 'Here's your partner. Make it work.'"

In fact, Jenna said the pairing is often a secret until the last minute.

"They really want to keep it a secret until you meet them live," Jenna said on The Morning After. "They want that genuine reaction. So I think people always think we know who we have and we're keeping it a secret. Absolutely not. They do not tell us. They really don't even want us to know the cast. It gets leaked a lot, but they want it very hush-hush until you walk in and meet your partner."

As for what the Dancing With the Stars team looks for when making these matches?

"It's based on height, build and personality and compatibility," former showrunner Rob Wade told E! News in 2015. "We don't pair people who aren't going to get on. It's too intense. It's not like The Bachelor or something, we couldn't do that. That would just be miserable experience for the celebrity, for us and the viewer. You don't want to see two people who don't like each other and, quite frankly, we have made that mistake pairing people up who didn't get on so well."

How Often Do the Pros and Celebrities Practice on Dancing With the Stars?

Put simply, a lot."Every day we have four-hour rehearsals," Rylee Arnold, who was partnered with Olympic gymnast Stephen Nedoroscik on season 33, shared on a September 2024 episode of the Lightweights Podcast With Joe Vulpis. "It’s either 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., 1:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. or 5:00 p.m to 9:00 p.m."But the work doesn't stop once the rehearsal wraps. Rylee noted she might then meet with producers or the creative team, work on choreography or study dance videos."Literally my whole life is devoted to it," she continued, "but it's my passion and it's what I love. So, it makes me so happy."Indeed, it's a no-days-off kind of gig."We have our show day on Tuesday and then it's Wednesday to Sunday, straight rehearsals," Rylee added. "And then Monday we have camera blocking and then Tuesday's show day again."

Do the Pros Get to Pick the Songs Each Week for Their Dance With Their Celebrity Partner?

"Mostly yes," Emma Slater and Britt Stewart revealed in a September 2025 Instagram video, "though it's a collaboration with producers."

What's the Process Like for Making the Costumes for Dancing With the Stars?

If you thought the quickstep was fast, just wait until you hear about the pace of the costume department."We meet with the set and lighting designers, dancers and talent and create a story [for each pair]," costume designer Daniela Gschwendtner told TV Insider back in 2017. "Then we sketch out ideas. We have five days, max, to make all the outfits. That’s half a day per costume, not including all the rhinestones. The fitting and trimming we do later. We have about 20 people in our department and then we have a separate tailor shop. It’s a big enterprise."In fact, costume designer Steven Norman Lee said pairs usually try on their costumes for the first time just hours before showtime. And while the department "might use a pair of pants again for the boys," he continued, everything is generally made custom each week.As Gschwendtner added, "We do reuse things for group numbers or promo shoots, but not for the competition. We don’t reuse things unless there’s a specific reason to do so. We try to keep everybody fresh and new in something different every week, so it stays interesting."

#756. Bruno Mars Announces Death of Dad in Heartbreaking Post

Bruno Mars shared that his dad Peter Hernandez died at the age of 74, writing in an emotional tribute, "In my eyes he was the greatest dad in the world."

Bruno Mars knows his dad was amazing, just the way he was.

The “That’s What I Like” shared that his father Peter Hernandez died at the age of 74 and shared a heartfelt tribute to the impact he had on his life.

“Last week I got to hug my father one last time,” Mars wrote on Instagram Nov. 19. “If you’ve ever seen me talk about him I’ve always said that he’s the man that taught me everything I know, especially when it comes to music.”

The 41-year-old—whose real name is also Peter Hernandez—added that his father helped raise six children, including Mars, his sisters Tiara, Tahiti, Presley and Jaime and his brother Eric, saying, “In my eyes he was the greatest dad in the world, and I will miss him everyday until we meet again.”

Mars—whose mother Bernadette San Pedro Bayot died from a brain aneurysm in 2013 at the age of 55—concluded his message by writing, “I Love you Pops. Kiss mom up there for me.”

Alongside the emotional message, the “Just the Way You Are” singer shared a photo of himself and his father sharing an embrace in a hospital bed along with several pictures of his father from throughout the years. He did not confirm his father’s cause of death.

Mars and his dad had shared a truly special bond through the years as the “Uptown Funk” singer’s love of music was inspired by his father’s own history of performing. While Hernandez was born in Brooklyn, he later moved to Hawaii, where he founded a doo-wop revival group called The Love Notes.

And from a young age, Hernandez—who split from Mars’ mother when the Grammy winner was 12—knew that his son was destined for greatness.

“He was a ham,” Hernandez told MidWeek about Mars in 2014. “As soon as he could walk and express himself, he had to be in the middle of everything and wanted to be a part of whoever he’d seen on TV.”

Of course, he was incredibly proud that his son was “the product of a lot of love from all his family.”

“No woman could ever love Bruno as much as his late mother did,” he added, “and no man could ever love Bruno as much as I love him.”

And Hernandez was there for his son right until the end, offering Mars advice on what to say when he was honored with a Las Vegas street named after him in April.

“He says, ‘My loving son, I know you don't like advice, but getting a street named after you is a monumental moment,’” Mars recounted in a video from the event shared by AP News. “‘I just wanna say, I know you must be very proud, ‘cause I’m so proud for you. If you are gonna say anything on the mic to the crowd, both God and people love humility. So be humble and tell your fans it's their street, and you're so honored and grateful.’”

#755. Hear Hans Zimmer’s Sweeping Take on Rüfüs Du Sol’s Classic ‘Innerbloom’

"Innerbloom XI" is out today, Nov. 20, the 11-year anniversary of the original's release.

Rüfüs Du Sol‘s emotional banger “Innerbloom” is well-established dance world canon, having provided the soundtrack to weddings, anniversaries, birthdays, engagements and other extra special moments since its release on Nov. 20, 2015 — eleven years ago today.

Today (Nov. 20) the already epic track becomes even more so under the watch of legend Hans Zimmer, who’s just released his take on the song in collaboration with Rüfüs du Sol and Bleeding Fingers, the scoring collective Zimmer co-founded to make music for films.

This version, “Innerbloom XI,” maintains the nine-minute length of the original, but takes the song to Zimmer’s characteristically sweeping cinematic scale, adding strings, percussion, xylophone, a choir and layers (and layers) of other instrumentation that makes the song fit squarely among Zimmer’s unparalleled Academy Award-winning body of work.

“Innerbloom XI” is accompanied by a new film from Rüfüs’s longtime creative director Katzki, made in collaboration with visual artist Thomás Blanchard that recreates the music video for the original. Watch the “Innerbloom XI” music video below.

Coming from Rüfüs’ du Sol’s second album, 2016’s Bloom, “Innerbloom” has generated 290 million official on-demand U.S. streams and a billion official on-demand global streams, according to Luminate. The song was a major highlight of the group’s recent Inhale/Exhale tour, a global two-year run that became nothing less than the biggest electronic tour of all time.

Beyond this “Innerbloom XI” project, new music from Zimmer will next be heard in the third installment of the Dune franchise, which is in theaters Dec. 18.

#754. You Actor Alexander Haskin Dies at Santa Monica Pier

Alexander Haskin, a personal trainer who became a background actor after leaving the Air Force, died Nov. 15 at the age of 38 after entering the ocean near the Santa Monica Pier, according to police.

Police are investigating the tragic death of Alexander Haskin.

The 38-year-old—who appeared as a background actor on shows like You and The Rookie—was pronounced dead Nov. 15 shortly after he was pulled from the ocean outside the Santa Monica Pier in Los Angeles, the Santa Monica Police Department confirmed to The Los Angeles Times.

Police said they received a report at 4:06 p.m. Nov. 15 that a man was in the water. Harbor guards responded and removed Haskin from the ocean, hoisting him onto the pier deck, where the Santa Monica Fire Department paramedics continued lifesaving measures, police spokesperson Lt. Lewis Gilmour told the Times.

Despite their efforts, Haskin was pronounced dead shortly before 5 p.m.

The actor’s cause of death was deferred, pending further investigation, according to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s Office records obtained by the Times.

Meanwhile, Gilmour confirmed an investigation into Haskin’s death is underway, though he said a preliminary investigation found no suspicious circumstances.

Plus, police confirmed that Haskin had been alone in the moments before entering the water, despite reports that he had been in an altercation with another person.

“The evidence shows the man was alone and did not interact with anyone in the period immediately before the incident,” Gilmour told the Times. “Security footage corroborates that finding.”

Following Haskin’s death, his dad Dana Haskin told the Times that his son had seemed in good spirits when they last spoke on Nov. 13. He also shared that Haskin had sent him a short text the morning of his death, though he did not disclose the message’s contents.

He also remembered his son—an Air Force veteran and personal trainer—as a “multifaceted guy” who loved music, fitness and acting.

“He was a happy guy,” Dana Haskin told the Times. “He liked to joke around, and he was always getting in trouble, but in a good way.”

#753. Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

Crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

The findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy

To test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

The birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent."

The results showed that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds

The team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an important role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

The recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

These signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," says Andreas Nieder.

Unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as quickly as primates.

The researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially important for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

However, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

#752. Traitors: New Blood Crowns Winner After Tearful Final Moments

Traitors: New Blood revealed which contestant walked away with the prize pot during the Alan Cumming-hosted reality show’s two-part finale, which aired Nov. 19 on NBC.

Content warning: This story contains spoilers for the finale of The Traitors: New Blood.

One by one, the Faithful fell—and a new Traitors winner was crowned.

Ironworker Shane Beatty hammered out his spot in TV history when he became the sole winner of The Traitors: New Blood, the fifth season of the U.S. series, during the emotional two-part finale on Nov. 19.

Beatty, 32, made history as the first recruited Traitor to win the U.S. series. He joined Katie Fites in the turret after she recruited him in the Nov. 12 episode, following two consecutive Traitor banishments.

Thursday night’s two-part finale began with the banishment of Jay Vinnedge and the murder of Clyde Moser—two Faithfuls who had begun voicing suspicions about Beatty and Fites.

After the remaining contestants completed their final mission, the two Traitors survived the castle’s final Round Table, which ended with Kriste Lewis’ banishment.

Five contestants remained for the final banishment ceremony, but they all chose to continue banishing. Fites was sent out of the game, visibly shocked when Beatty turned against her. In the final vote, Victor Vollbrechthausen was banished, despite Beatty’s attempt to keep him in the game until the end.

With only three contestants left, Beatty revealed to Faithfuls Wyatt Gillespie and Abbey Benjamin that he was a Traitor before breaking down in tears.

“I’m sorry,” Beatty said, his face in his hands. “I’m so sorry, guys.”

Beatty explained that he had started the game as a Faithful but was given an ultimatum to either become a Traitor or be murdered. Despite their visible devastation, Gillespie and Benjamin embraced Beatty.

“You don’t got to explain it, bro,” Gillespie said. “I would’ve done the same.”

With the $246,300 prize pot before him, Beatty told host Alan Cumming that the winnings were life-changing.

“I can finally just feel like I’m not drowning under the water,” Beatty said. “I just feel like I’m barely making it, and I can change my life now.”

The Traitors: New Blood premiered in September as the first all-civilian season of the U.S. series.

The next season of The Traitors will premiere Jan. 14, 2027 on Peacock and will return to an all-celebrity cast, including Olympian Chloe Kim, The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City’s Bronwyn Newport and The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ Whitney Leavitt.

Read on for more secrets of the Traitors castle...

1. While scheming is certainly a hallmark of The Traitors gameplay, contestants have no choice when it comes to their Traitors vs. Faithful status. Though, starting with season two, stars like Phaedra Parks and Kate Chastain were able to plead their case to host Alan Cumming.

"That has a really big bearing on it, as does Alan’s opinion,” executive producer Mike Cotton noted to Variety. "It’s almost like a job interview to be a Traitor, and we take all of that into account and decide just before the pick who that should be. We want to make sure we’ve got an interesting mix of characters that will bring their own unique skill set to it."

Though it’s not immediately clear to the cast just how many among them are Traitors. "We knew that there could potentially be three to five Traitors in the game,” Survivor’s Cirie Fields told E! News in 2023 after her season one victory. "That was explained to us from the very beginning."

2. They were also instructed to commit to the Traitors oath: "Do you commit to lie and deceive throughout the game? Are you willing to murder your fellow players every single night? And, do you vow to keep your identity and the identity of your fellow players a secret?"

3. To help producers determine who might be best at backstabbing and bluffing, contestants take a personality test. "We see attributes that might make someone a good liar or particularly deceptive,” Cotton Variety. Still, "We actually don’t know who the Traitors are until that pick, where Alan walks around and taps them on the shoulder.”

4. As for Cumming, he was excited to sign on for his campy role and bring his little dog, too. Recounting the initial pitch to Daily Beast in 2023, "I said, 'It’s sort of like you want me to be like a Bond villain. And I should actually bring my dog and pet her.’ And they went, 'That’s a good idea' And I thought, oh, I want to do this.”

With rescue pup Lala on hand, he leaned hard into his role, quoting playwright William Shakespeare and philosopher Plato on-camera. "So I had this flaring-nostril sort of persona,” he told the outlet. "And you’re kind of making stuff up as you go along. Literally, sometimes, they’re feeding me lines in my ear. So it was a bit like doing stand-up comedy actually, because you’re just winging it."

5. The cast might have a royally good time in Scotland’s Ardross Castle, but they don’t actually get their own palace digs.

"None of us stayed in the castle,” Cumming divulged to the Daily Beast. Instead, he continued, "You come to Scotland, and you stay in the Inverness airport hotel." While he had his own nearby digs, "I had a room in the castle where I would get made up and dressed," he added. "It had a huge bed in it. So I did actually sleep quite often, but not overnight."

6. In fact, the cast almost navigated rougher seas. "My first idea was to do it on a ship in Australia, and if somebody had to be out of the game, he or she had to jump into the water and swim to an island," creator Marc Pos revealed to Variety, "but then I thought it would be too difficult to produce."

7. Contestants weren’t able to wade into every corner of the castle. "We use a section of it," Cotton explained to Variety. "We’ve taken a wing of the castle, and that’s their area that they can play the game within. They’ve got all the outside as well. They’re free to roam around."

But with enough square footage for some 30 bedrooms, he noted, "If we covered that huge space, it’d be impossible to cover them all. They can split up and have their own conversations, but it’s small enough that someone could be listening on the door outside, and someone can see when someone disappears and has their own secret chat."

8. Perhaps that’s why Big Brother alum Rachel Reilly shared that car rides to and from the challenges were the most ideal times to scheme with fellow players. "You’re separated, and nobody can hear what you’re saying," she explained to Reality Blurred. "In the castle, you have to whisper."

9. Game planning at the hotel, however, was strictly verboten. "You’re not supposed to talk about the game when the mics aren’t ready or the cameras aren’t on," season two player Dan Gheesling told Business Insider, "because if we say something that’s important and it’s not on camera, they can’t use it on the show."

10. Also not allowed, season three’s Chrishell Stause revealed, was a hair and makeup team. "I would’ve died to have glam in the castle,” she told Us Weekly, "but Alan [did] not allow us to."

11. In order to arrange the nightly murders, "It’s a massive military operation each night to get the Faithful to bed in individual rooms," Cotton told Variety, "and get the Traitors back out to have their meeting."

Even season two then-couple Larsa Pippen and Marcus Jordan weren’t able to share a room. "I think they would have wanted to," acknowledged executive producer Sam Rees-Jones, "but they weren’t allowed to because it would have given them a foot up in the game."

12. Still, Shahs of Sunset’s Reza Farahan attempted to get crafty. "I did try to sneak out of my room to leave notes… I was trying to have fun in the moments where you weren't supposed to have fun," he told Digital Spy. "I would leave notes under people’s doors that said, 'I know what you did last summer, signed The Traitors.'"

13. Not that there is all that much time for fun and games. "We mainly like to film an episode a day, which is quite a big undertaking," Rees-Jones detailed to Variety. "But the reason we like to do that is because it keeps an immersive bubble, keeps their heads in the game. Schedule-wise, it’s a real pressure, but content-wise, it’s definitely the right thing to do. We start the day with breakfast, have a roundtable, have a mission, have a murder and then start again." (Stause revealed there was one night they got back to their rooms at 2 a.m.)

While the breakfasts are a strategic operation where players are brought in at staggered intervals, Cotton told Variety, the meals last "from start to finish, an hour max."

14. Perhaps that’s why producers take strides to keep contestants sharp. "You can only drink one drink a night," Love Island winner Ekin-Su Culculoglu, a season two Faithful, told Entertainment Weekly in 2024, "it was quite restricted."

15. Though it can be hard to find true allies in-game, each player is assigned a welfare team member. "They’re checking on you at all times,” season two standout Mercedes Javid said on the Just Sayin’ podcast. "They’re so cheerful and professional. I felt taken care of at all times."

16. As for forming onscreen bonds, contestants don’t know who they’ll be competing alongside until they arrive in Scotland. "You don’t want them to be able to research each other," casting director Deena Katz explained to Time, "or talk to each other or form alliances before." But once the game kicks off, players receive cheat sheets on each other and a journal to take notes.

17. For the record, Cumming fancies himself a Traitor. "I think it’d be great to decide who to murder," he told the Daily Beast in 2023. "The thing about this game—people would sort of turn on people and say, 'Well, they did this and therefore that means they’re a Traitor.' Well, they’re a Traitor because I patted them on the shoulder. And that’s the only reason they’re a Traitor."
