#722. A giant icy world hiding beyond Pluto could be our sixth dwarf planet

An enormous icy world discovered beyond Pluto could soon become the sixth officially recognized dwarf planet in our solar system.

The object, temporarily named 2026 ED138, was identified by an astronomer analyzing observations from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Early estimates suggest it ranks among the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found beyond Neptune. If its status is confirmed, it would join the five dwarf planets currently recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.

The discovery was announced at a press conference featuring Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, and Mario Jurić, a University of Washington astronomy professor who leads Rubin's solar system team. Holman made the initial discovery, while Jurić helped gather the additional evidence needed to verify it.

"If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman said. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for 10 years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach."

"Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation," Jurić said. "It's the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope."

How Astronomers Discovered the Hidden World

The breakthrough occurred on the evening of October 13, when Holman examined observations gathered by Rubin earlier in 2026. He was using specialized software developed with his colleague Kevin Napier to search for previously unidentified objects moving through the solar system.

The program compares billions of telescope detections, looking for individual points of light that appear in multiple observations and move in ways that suggest they belong to the same object. When the software identified ED138, Holman quickly realized that its apparent brightness and enormous distance pointed to something unusually large.

"My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Holman said. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong."

To check the finding, Jurić examined Rubin's stored observations and located 20 additional detections of ED138, including some captured as early as March 2026. The researchers then searched historical records from other astronomical surveys and identified images of the object dating back to 2016.

Together, these observations allowed the team to reconstruct more than a decade of the distant world's orbital motion, strengthening the evidence that the discovery was genuine.

Could This Be Our Solar System's Sixth Dwarf Planet?

ED138 currently lies approximately 46 astronomical units (au) from the Sun. One astronomical unit represents the average distance separating Earth and the Sun. By comparison, Pluto's average orbital distance is about 40 au.

Because ED138 travels beyond Neptune, astronomers classify it as a trans-Neptunian object (TNO). These distant bodies are valuable to scientists because their physical properties and orbital paths preserve clues about the solar system's distant past.

By examining their sizes, compositions, and movements, researchers can better understand how the solar system developed, how its giant planets shifted positions, and how smaller bodies were redistributed during that process.

However, being a trans-Neptunian object does not automatically make ED138 a dwarf planet. An essential requirement is that the object's gravity must be strong enough to shape it into a nearly round body.

Using measurements of ED138's brightness and distance, along with estimates of how much sunlight its surface reflects, astronomers calculate that it could measure anywhere from 600 to 1,500 kilometers across.

An icy object within that size range would generally be expected to have enough gravity to become round. Nevertheless, scientists will need more observations to establish ED138's actual dimensions and determine whether it qualifies as a dwarf planet.

Why Such a Massive World Remained Undiscovered

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is how an object this large managed to escape detection for so long.

ED138 occupies a region of the sky near the plane of the Milky Way, where millions of stars create an exceptionally crowded background. Against that dense field of light, the distant object's faint movement was difficult for earlier telescopes and surveys to distinguish.

Rubin Observatory has an important advantage. Its ability to repeatedly observe the Southern Hemisphere sky, combined with advanced computer algorithms, makes it possible to search enormous quantities of astronomical data for subtle changes in the positions of objects.

By examining millions or even billions of individual light detections, these systems can recognize the movement of small solar system bodies that might otherwise disappear into the surrounding stars. This capability was essential to finding ED138 in such a challenging part of the sky.

Rubin Observatory Could Reveal More Hidden Worlds

The newly identified object adds to a growing collection of solar system discoveries made by Rubin Observatory as it began gathering observations ahead of its ambitious Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), which officially started in June 2026.

Even before the survey began, the observatory was producing remarkable results. In April, Rubin's solar system researchers reported observations of more than 11,000 previously unknown asteroids, including approximately 380 new trans-Neptunian objects.

The team described that enormous collection of discoveries as "the tip of the iceberg," anticipating that the full survey would uncover many more objects. The identification of ED138 offers an early indication of just how significant those future findings could be.

Rubin's combination of extensive sky coverage, sensitivity, and rapid observations is also changing how astronomers investigate new discoveries. Once an object has been identified, researchers can search older telescope images to find instances when it was photographed but went unrecognized.

"Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision," Jurić said. "And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and 'precover' objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system."

As Rubin continues surveying the southern sky over the next decade, astronomers expect its observations to uncover additional objects that previous searches missed, potentially revealing more large, icy worlds in the outer solar system.

Anyone interested in exploring ED138 can view its location and orbit using Orbitviewer, an interactive web-based application that displays the solar system in three dimensions and allows users to explore its structure in real time.

Operations of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory are funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science.

#721. ‘Adolescence’ Breakout Owen Cooper Leads New Music Video for Beatles Hit ‘In My Life’

The film swings between the '60s and the current day, with Cooper's character touring the iconic sights of Liverpool.

Owen Cooper can officially add a Beatles music video to his (already) long list of accolades.

The 16-year-old, an Emmy, BAFTA and Golden Globe-winning actor for his performance in Netflix’s Adolescence, stars in a new video for the John Lennon-authored “In My Life.”

Directed by Olivier Award-winning Jessica Swale and Irina Alexiu, the film swings between the ’60s and the current day, with Cooper touring Liverpool — hitting the city’s iconic Royal Liver Building, the Anglican Cathedral, the Royal Albert Dock and Strawberry Field — playing music, and celebrating with family and friends across two different generations. It coincides with the recently released special edition of Rubber Soul, The Beatles‘ groundbreaking 1965 album, newly mixed by Giles Martin and Sam Okell. Related Stories Movies Social Media Bans in Tallinn Focus: Should Film Studios and Marketers Panic? Movies "Learn From the Mistakes of Mentors": The Head of Tallinn's Discovery Campus Is All About Bridging Film Education and Industry

Apple Corps — guardian of the iconic band’s legacy, intellectual property and creative ventures — have dropped the video shortly after announcing ambitious plans for Liverpool, including a new, 100,000 square-foot home for The Beatles Story opposite Liverpool Lime Street station.

It will be the first official fan experience to be operated in Liverpool by the company, releasing in time with Sam Mendes’ “four-film cinematic event” starring Paul Mescal, Harris Dickinson, Joseph Quinn and Barry Keoghan as Paul McCartney, John Lennon, George Harrison and Ringo Starr, respectively. The movies are currently slated for release in April 2028. A number of the new immersive locations will be created using sets and props from Mendes’ biopics.

“I love Liverpool. It’s part of who I am, it’s part of who The Beatles are,” said Paul McCartney when the news was announced. “If you’d told us this was going to happen when we were hanging out and getting started, we’d never have believed it. The extraordinary plans the Apple Corps team have shown me for The Beatles Story take me right back to that journey, from Liverpool to the world and back home again.”

#719. Werner Holzer Prize awarded to Katja Gloger and DW's Jaafar Abdul Karim

DW journalist Jaafar Abdul Karim and Russia correspondent Katja Gloger have been awarded the prestigious Werner Holzer Prize for international journalism.

At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.

Presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most important hot spots and championing international journalism.

At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.

In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades.

Second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.

A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.

"Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin."

At the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press. That shows what's at stake," she said.

The prize winner also said she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom.

In his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim said journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany.

Such pressure, he said, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.

"I firmly believe in the power of dialogue, today more than ever. That's why we must talk to one another. Even when it gets difficult. Even when we disagree. Or perhaps precisely because of that," he said.

Listening doesn't mean agreeing, and understanding doesn't mean being in agreement. "Especially now, in times of polarization, when those who believe they're always right are often the loudest, we as journalists have a special responsibility. When everyone is just shouting into their own bubbles or communities, we need journalists who connect these bubbles with one another," he said.

The jury praised Abdul Karim for creating programs at DW that reach millions of young people across the Arab world and in Germany. "His journalism fosters dialogue between countries, between generations, and between religions. He has set new standards," the jury stated.

So far in 2026, JaafarTalk has already garnered more than 1.1 billion views across all platforms, and its community has grown to more than 9 million followers. Its motto: "Diversity fosters dialogue."

"We need fact-based journalism that promotes dialogue and reflects the diversity of our society," Abdul Karim stressed. "By that, I mean an honest and open dialogue in which we do not look away or remain silent. On the contrary, we must take a clear stand against racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, discrimination, sexism, and hate speech — no matter which side they come from."

This article was originally written in German.

The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut.

Dream Chaser just received U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval for its return to Earth on that robotic mission, either at the space shuttle landing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida or at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.

"Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation," representatives of Sierra Space, the Colorado company that builds Dream Chaser, wrote on X on Monday (Nov. 9).

The FAA's environmental assessment found that Dream Chaser "would not significantly impact the quality of the human environment" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the agency stated. (It should also be noted that the U.S. has lately been suggesting that environmental laws should be bypassed to meet quickly rising demand for launches and landings.)

For example, for a potential return at Vandenberg, "sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited to 1.1 PSF [pounds per square foot] or less, which is similar to a thunderclap," the FAA stated.

The 30-foot-long (9 meters) Dream Chaser has been in development for more than two decades. It has yet to launch to space, though it has completed a couple of drop tests from the air. Dream Chaser was an entrant in NASA's Commercial Crew series of contracts to ferry astronauts to and from the International Space Station (ISS), but it didn't end up making the cut; in 2014, NASA picked Boeing's Starliner and SpaceX's Crew Dragon to provide this taxi service.

The following year, Sierra Nevada Corporation — then the entity in charge of Dream Chaser — unveiled a cargo version of the space plane. In 2016, NASA selected the company to conduct at least six uncrewed cargo flights to the ISS, but development delays repeatedly pushed those missions into the future.

Dream Chaser was originally expected to fly those robotic resupply missions on United Launch Alliance's workhorse Atlas V rocket. A few years ago, however, the space plane switched over to Vulcan Centaur, the successor to the venerable Atlas V.

Dream Chaser was supposed to ride on Vulcan's second-ever mission but wasn't ready in time, so that flight went ahead in October 2024 without the space plane. Sierra Space is now targeting spring 2027 for Dream Chaser's first liftoff, which will be a free-flying test mission in Earth orbit.

The company is now pursuing many types of contracts for Dream Chaser, anticipating a mix of missions for NASA, the U.S. military and private companies — including the consortiums that plan to build commercial space stations. Indeed, Sierra Space is a member of one such consortium — the group that plans to build an outpost known as Orbital Reef.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#717. Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins

A new study from the University of Otago, Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka, has revealed a surprising divide in the fortunes of one of New Zealand's least understood penguin species. Although Erect-crested penguins breed in just two remote island groups, their populations are experiencing dramatically different outcomes.

Published in PLOS ONE, the research found that one population has remained stable for at least 25 years, while the other has declined by more than 40 percent over the past three decades.

The study was led by Dr. Thomas Mattern of the Tawaki Project, which brings together scientists from the university's Departments of Zoology and Marine Science. Researchers also collaborated with the Antarctic Research Trust and the Global Penguin Society.

Drone Surveys Reveal a Surprising Penguin Population Divide

Erect-crested penguins breed exclusively on the Bounty and Antipodes islands, two isolated island groups located approximately 800 kilometers southeast of New Zealand's South Island.

To determine how many penguins remain, researchers conducted extensive drone surveys between 2022 and 2024. They photographed and counted every breeding colony across both island groups, producing the first comprehensive population survey of the entire species.

"The results overturn a long-standing assumption," Dr. Mattern says.

"The tiny Bounty Islands, at just 50 hectares, were found to hold almost as many breeding pairs (about 27,800) as the Antipodes Islands (about 29,800), even though the latter is 40 times larger and historically considered the species' stronghold."

The difference in population trends was even more unexpected. Despite their small size, the Bounty Islands have maintained a relatively consistent number of breeding penguins for decades. Meanwhile, the much larger Antipodes Islands have experienced a substantial decline.

"Comparing the new counts with historical records going back to the mid-1990s, the Bounty Islands population has remained essentially unchanged for at least 25 years.

"The Antipodes Islands population, by contrast, has declined by more than 40 percent since 1995."

Why Are Penguins Disappearing From the Antipodes Islands?

Researchers believe several overlapping pressures may explain why the two populations are heading in opposite directions. Natural predators, increasingly destructive storms, and differences in where the birds travel and feed could all be contributing.

One particularly troubling factor involves skuas, native subantarctic birds that prey on penguin eggs and chicks. As penguin colonies become smaller, the birds lose some of the protection that comes from nesting together in large numbers.

"As Antipodes colonies have shrunk over recent decades, the collective defense they once provided against native subantarctic bird, the skua, a natural predator of eggs and chicks, has weakened, allowing predation losses to increase and colonies to fragment further."

Co-author Dr. Klemens Pütz of the Antarctic Research Trust suggests that changes involving another penguin species may have intensified this pressure.

Eastern Rockhopper penguins suffered a "catastrophically" severe population collapse during the second half of the 20th century. Similar declines occurred across their Southern Ocean breeding range, likely driven by warming ocean waters. Today, fewer than 1,000 breeding pairs remain on the Antipodes Islands.

"As Rockhoppers disappeared, skuas may have turned to Erect-crested penguin eggs and chicks instead," Dr. Pütz says.

Stronger Storms and Different Migration Routes Add to the Threat

Predators are not the only challenge facing the Antipodes penguins. Increasingly powerful storms, consistent with wider climate trends across the Southern Ocean, have caused landslides that break up breeding colonies and leave the birds more vulnerable.

Differences in ocean habitats and seasonal movements may also help explain why the two populations have experienced such contrasting outcomes.

According to Dr. Mattern, penguins breeding on the Antipodes Islands migrate considerable distances into the Antarctic Polar Frontal Zone when the breeding season ends. In contrast, birds from the Bounty Islands remain closer to their nesting grounds, where the surrounding waters are more sheltered and may offer more abundant food.

These differences could leave the two populations exposed to very different environmental pressures, despite belonging to the same species.

The Strange Paradox of Schrödinger's Penguin

The researchers have named this unusual situation "Schrödinger's Penguin," drawing inspiration from the famous physics thought experiment involving a cat inside a sealed box.

In that experiment, the cat is imagined to be both alive and dead until the box is opened and its condition is observed. But Dr. Mattern explains that the penguin discovery turns the familiar concept around.

"With Schrödinger's cat, opening the box settles the question one way or the other.

"With Erect-crested penguins, it's the opposite. From a distance, without proper surveys, everyone assumed there was a single answer for the whole species.

"Once we actually opened the metaphorical box and looked, we found there wasn't one state at all, but two: stable on the Bounty Islands, declining on the Antipodes Islands."

In other words, looking at the species as a whole can conceal what is happening within individual populations. Only by examining both island groups separately did researchers uncover how dramatically their circumstances differ.

A Hidden Conservation Crisis for Endangered Penguins

The Erect-crested penguin is currently one of only four penguin species worldwide classified as "Endangered" on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List. Another New Zealand penguin, the hoiho/yellow-eyed penguin, shares that designation.

However, the two species have received very different levels of attention. While the plight of the hoiho has attracted ongoing public interest and conservation efforts, the Erect-crested penguin has remained relatively overlooked.

Dr. Mattern explains that the species' current conservation classification relies on population estimates from the 1970s that were considerably inflated. When the new survey results are considered, the "Endangered" designation remains broadly appropriate for the declining Antipodes population, but not for the stable Bounty Islands population.

This creates a difficult conservation dilemma. If the two populations are combined into a single assessment, the species' overall threat classification could actually improve, even though one population continues to decline sharply.

"Averaged across both populations, the global ranking would actually improve to "Vulnerable," masking the severity of the Antipodes decline, and downplaying how exposed the Bounty Islands, likely the species' last secure stronghold, are to industrial fishing."

The researchers warn that a more favorable overall classification could create a misleading impression of security. Although the Bounty Islands population remains stable, it may still face significant threats, particularly from industrial fishing activity.

"A single, ostensibly improved threat ranking is like putting the lid back on Schrödinger's box, trading a convenient illusion for the stronger protection the Bounty Islands population actually needs," Dr. Mattern says.

The findings highlight why conservation efforts must account for the circumstances of individual populations rather than relying exclusively on a species' global status. For Erect-crested penguins, recognizing the differences between the two island groups could be essential to protecting their future.

The study received funding from the Vontobel Foundation (Switzerland) through the Antarctic Research Trust and from the Global Penguin Society. The research was carried out under permits issued by the New Zealand Department of Conservation.

Materials provided by University of Otago. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#716. Bo Derek Is Still a ‘10’ at 70: “It All Worked Out, Didn’t It?”

Forty-seven years after the racy rom-com made her a generational sex symbol, Derek opens up about the surprising origins of her iconic braids, her scandalous first marriage and the Hollywood career she never really wanted

Bo Derek was 21 when she came bounding down a beach in a flesh-colored bathing suit, beaded cornrows bouncing on her shoulders. The movie was 10, Blake Edwards’ 1979 comedy about a film composer, played by Dudley Moore, who’s in the throes of a midlife crisis.

Ten is also roughly the number of minutes Derek appears onscreen. A lot more happens in the movie. Derek and Moore smoke up and get down to the rump-pa-pa-pump of Ravel’s “Boléro.” Julie Andrews, Edwards’ wife, plays Moore’s girlfriend and sings several songs.

The beach sequence ends with them crashing into each other. But no one remembers the slapstick part. They just remember Bo. A blond, blue-eyed California surfer girl, she managed to look all-American and exotic at the same time. A few seconds in slow motion were enough to make Derek a superstar and 10 a smash hit. The shot belongs alongside Rita Hayworth peeling off a glove in Gilda. Related Stories TV 'And Just Like That' Writers Compare Finale Reaction to Ending 'Sex and the City': "It Was the Opposite of a Heated Debate" TV Sarah Jessica Parker Responds to 'And Just Like That' "Hate-Watching" Trend: "I Guess I Don't Really Care"

On Nov. 20, Derek turns 70. She’s talking via Zoom from her ranch in the Santa Ynez Valley, just north of Santa Barbara, where she lives with her husband, John Corbett, 65, the easygoing star of Sex and the City and the My Big Fat Greek Wedding movies.

Rain is pounding outside the window behind her. Lying nearby is Bear, the 110-pound German shepherd who had previously belonged to Gene Hackman and wife Betsy Arakawa. Derek and Corbett adopted him after the couple died in early 2025 — a mutual publicist made the connection.

I ask her when she was happier: now or at the peak of her post-10 success?

Derek got her role in 10 thanks in part to Hugh Hefner. Her first husband, John Derek, was a good friend of Hef’s and spent a lot of time at the Playboy Mansion. Bo and John’s relationship caused a major scandal: They got together making a movie in Greece when he was 46 and she was only 16.

Bo was still just 16 the first time John brought her to the Playboy Mansion. According to Bo’s 2001 memoir, Riding Lessons, John showed Hef some photos he’d taken of his new girlfriend. “I’ve never seen anything I wanted to defile so much,” was his response. John told Bo to take it as a compliment. “He respected me,” she tells me of the Playboy founder. “We only talked about things that you might consider more important than the grotto.”

One night at the Mansion, John ran into Edwards, who told him he’d heard about Bo and thought she might be perfect for 10. He’d already seen hundreds of girls, and no one was quite right. John thought the rejection would do her good. He felt she lacked discipline when it came to her career. “I went in to meet Blake and came home with the part,” she writes.

She remembers the shoot with great fondness, particularly working with Edwards and the addition of the “brilliant” Moore, a last-minute casting change from George Segal, who clashed with the director.

The problems began after 10 had wrapped. The studio, Orion Pictures, didn’t have high hopes for it. But they negotiated a shoot with Life magazine, which was getting a reboot and wanted a young ingenue — a throwback to the days of putting up-and-comers like Hayworth and Marilyn Monroe on its cover.

The photographer assigned to the shoot was given strict orders: The magazine wanted to faithfully re-create vintage pinup shoots of Hollywood starlets, right down to Hayworth’s negligee and Monroe’s bed of red satin. They also wanted Derek to appear emerging out of a burlap sack for the actual cover photo. She hated the idea and stormed out of the shoot.

Derek, who was born in Long Beach and grew up surfing, was shopping for a new windsurfer in a store in Marina del Rey when, somehow, incensed Orion executives tracked her down. They demanded to be put on the surf shop’s speakerphone.

“At first it was pleading,” she recalls of their attempt to get her to return to the photo shoot. “Then it was threatening. Then I’d had enough. I wasn’t interested anymore.”

Edwards was overseas at the time, prepping his next movie. By the time she got home, Derek had a message waiting for her from his agent: “Blake is furious and you’ll never work for him again.”

Derek — 22 at the time and with no representation — demanded to see it in writing. And so she was sent a telegram stating that Edwards would never hire her again if she failed to do the promotional shoot for 10. The thing was, Edwards had an option on Derek for three more films. “So I got out of that,” she says.

The studio retaliated by cutting her out of the press materials and disinviting her to the movie’s premiere. But a TV spot featuring Derek aired during a hugely rated Muhammad Ali fight.

“It just started this buzz,” she recalls. “All of a sudden, people were trying to reach me, the press was trying to track me down.”

10 opened on Oct. 5, 1979, and became a box office smash, grossing $75 million domestically. (That year’s Alien made $79 million.) Derek, meanwhile, became an overnight sensation, with women around the world demanding the “Bo braids” from their hairdressers.

John Derek had suggested she spend the film with her hair slicked back — something that would stand out from the feathered hair Farrah Fawcett had made a sensation. They were shopping in Inglewood when they spotted the African American hairstyle and together thought it would be the perfect look for Jenny. One of Ann-Margret’s backup singers connected her with a braider in Compton. (The Viva Las Vegas star was an old family friend who had known Bo since childhood.)

“I only work from my dreams,” the braider told them, adding that she dreamed of a butterfly the night before, which served as the design’s inspiration. She also told them she had braided Cleopatra’s hair in a previous life.

In Riding Lessons, Derek remembers singer Roberta Flack criticizing her on The Phil Donahue Show for taking credit for a hairstyle Black women had worn for generations.

“For the record,” Bo writes, “I never, ever intended to take credit for the sensation that my hairdo caused.” There was a Bo Derek pinup poster in 1979, which featured her seductively kneeling in the surf, and a Bo Derek calendar by 1981.

All of this Bo-mania seemed to smooth things over with Orion. “All of a sudden, I start getting jewelry from the studio chairman, Arthur Krim,” Derek says. “I had people coming with suitcases of cash trying to get me to sign on the dotted line, telling me what I should and shouldn’t do.” Edwards, too, found it in his heart to forgive her, and the two remained friends until his death in 2010.

It wasn’t that Derek didn’t enjoy being famous. She was just less sure she wanted the career everyone else seemed to want her to have. She was in a hotel room in Paris when it all caught up with her.

“I remember sobbing and saying, ‘I’m so confused. I don’t know what to do,’ ” she says. “And my husband said, ‘Well, do what you want. Just because everybody would kill for this career doesn’t mean you have to love it.’ “

The handsome son of silent film actors, John Derek appeared in more than 50 films, most famously playing Joshua, a follower of Charlton Heston’s Moses, in 1956’s The Ten Commandments. When the roles dried up, he transitioned to independent filmmaking and photography, particularly of beautiful women. (He shot Bo’s 1980 Playboy cover and spread.)

“I said, ‘Well, I just want to go make little films like we were doing before,’ ” Derek continues. “So I called my agent Marty Baum, and he put together Tarzan.” A soft-core spin on the legend told from Jane’s point of view — the alternate title was Me, Jane — 1981’s Tarzan, the Ape Man was eviscerated by critics but a surprise hit at the box office, earning $37 million. Her husband directed it, while Bo also produced the film. “I cringe when I look at a lot of it now,” she says. “But it was beautiful. It was fun. It was a romp in the jungle.”

The first little film they made together was in Greece, another soft-core outing written and directed by John called Fantasies that involved an affair between a teenage girl and her adoptive brother. Bo, newly 16, was accompanied by her mother to the audition.

Bo went by Mary Cathleen Collins then. “He was the most beautiful man I had ever seen,” she writes of John in Riding Lessons. She adopted the nickname Bo shortly after John came into her life.

The 46-year-old John was married to Linda Evans at the time — his third wife, after Russian ballerina Pati Behrs and original Bond girl Ursula Andress. A TV actress since the 1960s, Evans was 30 at the time — Dynasty was still several years away — and was discouraged by John from pursuing acting work.

“She was beautifully independent,” Evans, now 84, recalls of Bo, adding that she had “zero, zero, zero” inkling her husband might have romantic designs on the teen.

At John’s encouragement, Evans gave the neophyte acting lessons several times a week at their home. Evans noticed the director and the ingenue would spar during rehearsals and worried the film would fall apart once they left for Greece.

When Evans arrived on set a few weeks into filming, she learned her husband had fallen in love with Bo. “To say I was devastated is an understatement,” she says.

Still, she never put the blame on Bo. “She didn’t break up my marriage,” Evans says. She’s equally emphatic about who pursued whom. “She did not go after him — he went after her.”

But she doesn’t hold much resentment for John, either. She describes him as an “exceptionally fascinating man” who wrote her a love letter every night for nine years. She’d wake up every morning and read it. “When he loved you, he was consumed with you.”

Once the press caught wind of the affair, it sparked a feeding frenzy. “They want you to be humiliated,” Evans says. “I refuse to be humiliated.”

While she held out hope John would come back and admit he made a huge mistake, that never transpired. She finally let go when he called her up at 3 a.m. one night and inquired if she was seeing anyone. “Oh my God,” Evans recalls. “I’m trying to figure out how to live here and he wants to know about dating.”

Evans thinks it all played out for a reason. “John didn’t want me to work a lot with other people,” says Evans, who went on to marry real estate executive Stan Herman in 1976. “He wanted me to mostly work with him. So if I’d stayed with John, I never would have done Dynasty.

“It was a favor they both did to me,” she continues, “because I ended up having an extraordinary life going off on my own.”

John took Bo from Greece to West Germany. He later told The Washington Post that he was concerned about statutory rape laws in the U.S. “It was definitely more acceptable there,” Bo says. They were married in the Wee Kirk Chapel in Las Vegas a few years later, a wheezing pug tucked under the minister’s arm. They spent their wedding night in an RV parked outside Caesars Palace. Bo was 19 and he was 49.

The following day, Bo set off for Newfoundland to play a victim in the Jaws knockoff Orca, her screen debut. (Producer Dino De Laurentiis offered her the part himself.) She’s listed in the closing credits as Bo Derek.

Bo has no children. I ask what she’d do if her own daughter came home with a man 30 years her senior. “If it were my daughter, I would have kidnapped her and taken her away from him, of course,” she says. “It’s not the natural way of things.

“At the same time,” she continues, “I was with him 25 years until he died. He was a very ridiculously honest, good man. And it all worked out, didn’t it?”

Bo never sustained a particularly memorable acting career. Edwards’ farce turned her into one of the most recognizable and desired women in the world, but her subsequent parts never lived up to her star power.

After Tarzan, the Ape-Man came Bolero in 1984 (whose title shamelessly capitalized on the famous scene from 10) and Ghosts Can’t Do It in 1990 — both of which were directed by her husband and disappointed at the box office. The films’ main draw involved Bo taking her clothes off.

Derek’s days as a leading lady mostly drew to a close by the early 1990s. She remained a fixture in popular culture over the decades, turning up in small roles on TV shows, in the occasional movie and in one startling cameo from 2015, playing Tara Reid’s mother in Sharknado 3: Oh Hell No!

“I didn’t always make the right career moves,” she says. “But God, it was fun.”

Corbett relishes telling the story of how he and Derek met.

It was 2002, and old-school agent Norby Walters, who lived in the apartment above him in West Hollywood, hosted Wednesday night poker games attended by the likes of Burt Reynolds, Sharon Stone, Richard Lewis and Harvey Korman.

Corbett was a regular attendee at those. But it was another celebrity get-together — Walters’ annual Oscar night party Night of 100 Stars — that brought him and Derek together.

The guy known to millions of Sex and the City fans as Aidan had no one to bring as a date. So Walters slid a sheet of paper under his door with the names of about 20 actresses on it.

“Give me your picks one through five,” Walters wrote.

Corbett circled Derek’s name and slid it under Walters’ door. Not long after, his phone rang.

Corbett was mostly kidding. He was an 18-year-old high school senior in Wheeling, West Virginia, when 10 came out. He never even saw the movie, but he remembers the newspaper photo — a black-and-white close-up of Derek that took up a half page of the Sunday paper.

“She’s sort of staring into the camera,” Corbett recalls. “I remember thinking, ‘My God, I wish I had a girlfriend that beautiful.’ “

The pair met first for a dinner in Beverly Hills to see if they would hit it off. They did — big time. On Oscar night, they hit the Walters party, attended by a less-sizzling set, then Derek got them into the much hotter Vanity Fair affair. The celebrity circuit was kind of foreign to Corbett, who spent most of his time in Seattle.

“I had filmed Big Fat Greek Wedding, but it wasn’t out yet,” he recalls. “But they knew me from Sex and the City. I got to be kind of famous at this party, which was kind of cool. And it felt good, too, to be showing that off in front of Bo. I liked it.”

When he dropped her off, they made plans to see each other again. “We’ve kind of never been apart since then, really,” he says. Early in their courtship, he finally got to see 10 when they rented it from a Blockbuster on Sunset Boulevard. “Bo’s never been better in anything,” he says, praising her “nuanced little looks” and line readings. They married quietly in late 2020.

She keeps a packed schedule. An avid equestrian, she was appointed in 2008 by Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger to the California Horse Racing Board, where she served until 2015, advocating for the safety of racehorses and jockeys. She’s still on the board of Del Mar racetrack.

Corbett says she recently spent two weeks on the road, traveling between Kentucky for the Breeders’ Cup, Washington, D.C., and New Jersey for a tribute to Dudley Moore. She’s flying to Finland this winter to see the northern lights on horseback. Corbett, meanwhile, is happier hanging at home with the dogs. “She just loves to be around people, man,” he says.

He was 40 and Bo was 45 when they met: “I just can’t believe how quickly my life has flashed in front of my eyes.”

I ask Derek what works so well between them.

“I fall in love,” she says. “I fall hard, and I think that when someone else truly loves you, it’s such a gift to cherish. It’s kind of a miracle with all the billions of people in the world, so I cherish it.”

When a call came about a year and a half ago saying a dog named Bear belonging to Gene Hackman and his wife, Betsy Arakawa, needed a happy home, the couple said no. They already had two German shepherds, and one was a rambunctious puppy. Then they saw a picture of Bear.

In police bodycam footage taken the day their bodies were discovered, an officer describes a dog holding vigil by Arakawa’s side. Corbett says it was Bear. The couple’s death was still a mystery at the time. It would turn out Arakawa died of hantavirus and Hackman, who suffered from Alzheimer’s, died a week later from heart disease.

Bear made the 17-hour trip from New Mexico in the back of a Ford Explorer. The couple has raised many German shepherds over the years — but none nearly as big as the massive creature who came bounding out of the trunk.

“Oh no,” Corbett recalls thinking. “What have we gotten ourselves into?” But Bear turned out to be a “perfect gentleman,” as Derek says, and loves to sing along whenever Corbett plays piano or guitar.

Her birthday will be a quiet one — just Bo and John and a few intimates over dinner. I ask if she has any regrets.

“No,” she says. “I tend to be an optimist. And I’m grateful to the industry. It’s been so good to me and I’ve made the most amazing friends around the world. It’s an embarrassment of riches, honestly.”

The new observatory managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short.

The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that launched in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24.

"I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas," Mikko Pöntinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki who made the initial discovery with a Solar System Objects Science Working Group within the Euclid Consortium, said in a statement.

Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something new to us.

Euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.

This finding shows that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

Astronauts' photos of innocuous space debris helped fuel belief in the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station, crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space.

Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you."

Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age.

According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the "Black Knight Satellite," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence.

So how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public?

Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signals while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs.

At the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth.

Another component that was later incorporated into the Black Knight Satellite mythos came to light in May 1954, when newspaper reports began publicizing author Donald Keyhoe's assertions that the U.S. Air Force had detected at least two unidentified satellites orbiting Earth.

At the time, Keyhoe claimed that U.S. government scientists at White Sands were reportedly "making an intensive effort to locate and chart the course of the satellites in an attempt to determine what they are and where they came from," as the author was quoted as saying in articles like one that appeared in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch on Friday, May 14, 1954.

However, later in August of that year, U.S. officials apparently concluded these objects were likely to have been meteors that became "satellites of the Earth and were revolving with it 400 to 600 miles out in space," and that Dr. Lincoln LaPaz, one of the preeminent experts on meteors at the time, had "definitely identified the objects as natural rather than man-made," as reported by the New York Times.

Just a few years later in February 1960, a similar story appeared in Time magazine, which this time alleged that the U.S. Navy had spotted an unidentified dark object in orbit that was suspected of being a Soviet reconnaissance satellite. This object was later identified as well, with officials determining it had likely been debris from the American spy satellite Discoverer 8.

Another similar claim suggests that on May 15, 1963, during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission, NASA astronaut Gordon Cooper allegedly observed an unusual object in space, which some accounts describe as a "glowing green object" that followed his capsule. While it is true that Cooper reported seeing what he characterized as "John’s fireflies," which were a reference to earlier sightings of unusual luminous objects made by astronaut John Glenn during the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, it was later concluded that the so-called "fireflies" resulted from small bits of ice separating from the spacecraft itself, which present a greenish hue as sunlight reflects off of them (audio of Cooper describing this during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission can be found here).

Beyond this, however, there is no evidence of Cooper observing any singular object during this mission, either in Cooper's personal records or mission audio and transcripts from the time.

Arguably, one of the most extraordinary components of the Black Knight Satellite theory involves its alleged age, which according to some theories places its initial entry into Earth's orbit as far back as 13,000 years ago. But if so, how would anyone know this, and what evidence could support such an idea?

Understanding this bizarre aspect of the Black Knight mythos requires a look back at the theories of Scottish writer Duncan Lunan, which he first proposed in 1973. At that time, Lunan was receiving international attention for his investigation into mysterious long-delayed echoes, proposing that one theory behind the phenomenon could be that they represented signals from Earth that were being rebroadcast from an extraterrestrial probe — an idea that borrowed from theories first proposed by Australian scientist Ronald Bracewell.

According to Lunan's theory, such a hypothetical "Bracewell probe" might have arrived in Earth's vicinity roughly 13,000 years ago after traveling from within a planetary system associated with the star Epsilon Boötis, some 236 light-years away.

Within just a few years, Lunan had withdrawn his conclusions, but this did little to prevent his initial ideas about a 13,000-year-old alien satellite from being incorporated into the growing mythos surrounding the alleged Black Knight Satellite.

That brings us back to what are arguably the most widely circulated images associated with the Black Knight satellite: the famous images from NASA's STS-88 mission taken by astronaut Jerry Ross in December 1998.

According to spaceflight historian James Oberg, the object in Ross's photos could indeed be positively identified as the thermal blanket lost during the mission, especially since he had specifically asked Ross about the incident — and later misinterpretations of his photos as being evidence of an alien spacecraft — during an October 2014 interview.

At that time, Oberg asked Ross whether he had time during the 1998 spacewalk "to gaze at [the thermal cover] and think about how it looked," to which Ross said no, admitting he had been "too pissed at myself to wonder what it looked like!"

When asked what advice he would offer to those who have misinterpreted the object in his photographs for being something more exotic and otherworldly, Ross told Oberg, "If we see something up there we will be the first ones to ask questions and to tell people we saw something we didn't understand."

"Conspiracy theories are fun for those working on them, but a waste of valuable brain power," Ross added.

But what, specifically, about the idea of an ancient extraterrestrial probe lurking in orbit around our planet makes this far-fetched theory so captivating?

"I think it's because this idea of an alien satellite kicking around in orbit checks so many conspiracy theory boxes," says Amy Shira Teitel, a spaceflight historian who has also tackled the Black Knight satellite theories in the past, and points to other misperceptions about space that have given rise to conspiracy theories over the years.

"People, for some reason, believe space is fake or that every mission is fake because the Van Allen Belts will kill you," Shira Teitel recently told Space in an email, while noting that most missions take place well within safe distances from the inner radiation belt, with notable exceptions that include the Gemini 11 mission, as well as lunar flights.

"People also love UFOs," she adds. "Even skeptics have a little bit of a soft spot for the idea of an alien craft flying by to say hi. I think when you take all these conspiracy threads together, the Black Knight sort of fits perfectly in that intersection!"

Overall, the bizarre story of the Black Knight satellite offers a textbook example of how a collection of unconnected events and speculative interpretations can gradually accumulate into a single narrative over time.

Despite this reality, belief in the existence of a mysterious ancient satellite lurking in orbit will likely persist for years to come, helping ensure its place as one of the most peculiar — and enduring — legends of the Space Age.

Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

#713. Physicists use laser light to unlock a crystal's hidden electrical powers

Physicists at Auburn University have discovered how to use brief bursts of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions hidden inside a crystal. Their findings shed new light on a mystery that has puzzled researchers for decades and demonstrate how lasers can influence the material's electrical behavior. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists explore faster ways to process and store information.

The research was led by Wencan Jin, the Thomas and Jean Walter Endowed Associate Professor in Auburn's Department of Physics, and graduate student Mohamed Kandil. Their paper, "Optical Poling of a Quantum Ferroelectric Metal across the Order-Disorder Phase Transition," received an Editors' Suggestion designation from Physical Review Letters. Scientists at Japan's National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology produced the crystals used in the study.

A Decades-Old Mystery Hidden Inside a Crystal

The researchers investigated a modified version of strontium titanate, a material with an unusual combination of electrical characteristics. Although electrons can travel through the crystal, it also contains extremely small regions with positive and negative electrical sides. Known as polar nanoregions, these microscopic "islands" can point in different directions or become aligned with one another. Understanding how and why this alignment occurs is essential to explaining the material's properties and learning how to manipulate them.

Scientists have spent decades trying to determine what happens when these regions become organized. One possibility is that atoms move together to produce the polarized state. Another is that the tiny electrical islands are already there and simply begin pointing in the same direction as temperatures fall. The distinction is similar to the difference between assembling a group of people and asking people who are already gathered to turn and face the same way. Because the regions are extraordinarily small and produce very weak signals, determining which explanation is correct has been a persistent challenge.

Laser Experiments Reveal How Electrical Order Emerges

To investigate, the Auburn researchers developed an exceptionally sensitive system that uses lasers to measure subtle changes in the crystal. By studying how the material altered incoming light, they were able to monitor the orientation of its electrical regions while repeatedly heating and cooling the sample.

The measurements revealed a clear pattern. At warmer temperatures, the tiny regions pointed in seemingly random directions. When the crystal cooled, however, they began adopting preferred orientations. This behavior provided compelling evidence that the electrical islands existed before becoming aligned, supporting the explanation that cooling organizes regions already present in the material.

A Flash of Light Creates Order in a Trillionth of a Second

The team went beyond observing this natural process. Researchers also demonstrated that short laser pulses could temporarily align the electrical islands, even at higher temperatures when the regions would ordinarily remain disorganized. Using an optical measurement, they were able to detect the pattern produced by the laser light.

The effect was extraordinarily brief, lasting approximately one picosecond, or one trillionth of a second. Nevertheless, the ability to create and detect this electrical alignment using light provides a promising approach for studying how information might be controlled at extremely high speeds.

Three Years of Experiments Lead to a Breakthrough

Achieving these results required considerable patience and technical refinement. The collaboration began at the 2023 American Physical Society March Meeting, where Jin met Japanese researchers capable of producing the specialized crystals needed for the experiments.

Back at Auburn, the team spent almost a year refining its equipment before it could reliably detect the weak optical signals from the tiny electrical regions. The next obstacle was even more demanding: measuring the extremely short interval during which laser illumination caused the regions to align.

"The breakthrough came in 2025, when Mohamed finally observed the disordered polar regions becoming aligned under laser illumination," Jin said. "Seeing that signal emerge was a thrilling moment for the team."

The achievement also represents an important personal milestone for Kandil, whose first published research paper reflects three years of dedicated experimental work.

"This experiment has truly been Mohamed's odyssey," Jin said. "It took him three years of dedication to complete the work and achieve his first publication."

New Possibilities for Ultrafast Information Technology

The discovery provides important evidence about how electrical order develops in this unusual crystal while also establishing a method for manipulating that order with light. Rather than simply observing the material's internal behavior, researchers can now briefly influence its microscopic electrical patterns and detect the resulting changes.

Although practical applications remain a future possibility, the experiments offer a new way to investigate the rapid electrical processes occurring inside quantum materials. By revealing how light can control these previously elusive patterns, the Auburn researchers have opened another avenue for exploring technologies that could one day transform how information is processed and stored.

Materials provided by Auburn University Department of Physics. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#712. Kristen Doute to Host Sports and Pop Culture Podcast ‘Run It Back’ in Partnership With PODGO (Exclusive)

'The Valley' star will co-host the show with Katie DiMento.

Reality television veteran Kristen Doute is channeling her passion for sports and knowledge of pop culture in the brand new podcast Run It Back, in partnership with PODGO.

Co-hosted with Katie DiMento, the video-first show will release new episodes weekly. Run It Back will blend together the intersection of sports and pop culture, creating a space for conversations in sports, entertainment, celebrity culture and everyday life to meet.

“From the NFL, Fantasy drafts and the biggest moments in the worlds of sports to Bravo drama, pop culture’s most viral moments, relationships, style and everything happening online, the hosts bring different perspectives, genuine expertise and plenty of personality to the conversation,” a description for the podcast further reads. “The result is an entertaining, accessible and opinionated take on the stories women are talking about, without assuming that sports knowledge and pop culture knowledge have to exist in separate worlds.” Related Stories Movies Lance Broadway, Pitcher Turned 'Olympus Has Fallen' Actor, Dies at 43 Business New York Knicks Star Josh Hart Inks Two-Book Deal With HarperCollins (Exclusive)

Doute is a seasoned reality TV star, first appearing in Bravo’s acclaimed Vanderpump Rules. A founding cast member of the series, she currently stars in its spinoff The Valley, which centers on former Vanderpump Rules stars and their new friend group tackling adulthood while living in the San Fernando Valley.

She is also the co-host of the Balancing Act podcast, which was originally branded as Sex, Love…and What Else Matters and launched in 2022.

“I’ve always loved sports, and growing up a Detroit football fan, Sundays have always been about the game, the passion and, of course, having a lot to say about it,” Doute said in a statement. “I’ve also always loved a good conversation, a little friendly debate and, let’s be honest, a little bit of drama. What makes Run It Back so fun is that we get to bring together two worlds that people don’t always think belong in the same conversation. Sports and pop culture are such a huge part of what we’re talking about every day, and women have plenty to say about both. Katie brings her sports knowledge and perspective, I bring my love of pop culture and my own sports fandom, and together we’re creating a space where we can be opinionated, laugh, disagree and say what everyone else is thinking.”

DiMento, a Boston native and sports authority, added, “Sports have always been such a big part of my life and for my family, and I’ve always loved the conversations, debates and personalities that come with being a fan. What I love about Run It Back is that we’re not putting sports and pop culture into separate boxes. They’re connected, they’re constantly influencing each other, and women are just as invested in those conversations as anyone else.”

“Kristen and I bring completely different perspectives, which makes for some really fun, honest and unexpected conversations,” she added. “This show is about having a voice, knowing your stuff, being curious and never feeling like you need permission to join the conversation.”

The partnership was brokered in collaboration with Maxx Lepselter of Maxx Mgmt, who represents the talent; Maxx Mgmt will identify and develop brand collaborations, sponsorships and marketing partnerships for Run It Back.

“We’re excited to have played a role in bringing this partnership together and helping Kristen and Katie launch Run It Back with PODGO,” Lepselter said in a statement. “Representing talent is about more than negotiating deals. It’s about identifying opportunities that align with their personalities, passions and long-term goals. This podcast brings together two dynamic voices with a unique perspective on sports and pop culture, and we see tremendous potential to build on that through strategic brand collaborations, sponsorships and marketing partnerships that extend well beyond the podcast itself.”

PODGO will handle distribution across major podcast platforms and manage advertising representation and sponsorship opportunities for the series.

“There’s such a natural connection between sports and pop culture, and women are already part of both conversations,” said Tristan Capes-Davis, founder of PODGO. “Kristen and Katie bring two distinct audiences and perspectives together in a way that feels authentic, entertaining and highly relevant. Kristen has an established relationship with a passionate reality-TV and pop-culture audience, while Katie brings the sports authority that gives the show a real point of difference. Run It Back has the personality, format and audience appeal to build something special, and PODGO is excited to help bring it to audiences everywhere.”

Run It Back will release new episodes weekly. Full video episodes will be available on YouTube and video podcast distribution across Spotify and Apple Podcasts, while short-form content and highlights will be distributed across social media at @runitbackwithKD across platforms.

The Leonid meteor shower peaks overnight tonight (Nov. 17-18), sending shooting stars racing across the night sky from the direction of the constellation Leo.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight (Nov. 17-18) sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle.

Up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation. NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell.

Leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026!

The best time to spot Leonids is in the hours before dawn on Nov. 18, when the radiant will reach its highest point in the southeastern sky, maximizing the amount of meteors that may be seen skimming through Earth's atmosphere. By then, the waxing moon will have set, leaving darker skies and a better chance of spotting fainter meteors.

Shooting stars that appear close to the radiant will strike Earth almost head-on, leaving the shortest trails. Instead, find a patch of sky a short distance away from the constellation Leo, where the meteors will be at their most impressive, and give your eyes 20-30 minutes to fully adapt to the dark.

As if shooting stars weren't enough, the Leonid shower is also known for spawning dazzling fireballs and long-lasting Earth-grazing meteors, which strike our atmosphere at an oblique angle, leaving long trains as they skim through before passing back out into space.

The shower is also capable of producing magnificent meteor storms when Earth passes through particularly dense trails of debris left behind by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.

Read more: 'It looked like every star in the sky was falling': Eyewitnesses remember the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966

Sadly, we'll have to wait a bit for the next big show. According to the Planetary Society, another Leonid meteor storm could occur as early as 2031, while a study released in August 2026 predicts potentially spectacular displays in 2033 and 2034.

Want to photograph a shooting star? Then be sure to read our guide to imaging shooting stars, along with our selections of the best lenses and cameras for astrophotography on the market in 2026.

Editor's Note: If you would like to share your Leonid photos with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

#710. Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago

Dinosaurs living along ancient coastlines may have enjoyed an unexpected addition to their diets: seaweed and other food from the ocean. New research suggests that marine resources washed onto prehistoric beaches helped feed dinosaurs and their prey millions of years ago.

Today, powerful storms frequently deposit seaweed and other ocean material along shorelines, creating opportunities for animals that live on land to find additional food. Scientists call this process marine subsidization (MS). It is especially common in coastal environments and can become more important when food on land is limited, such as during droughts.

A new study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution suggests that this relationship between land and sea existed during the age of dinosaurs. By examining chemical signatures preserved in fossils, researchers found evidence that ocean resources contributed to prehistoric food chains.

"We show that coastal terrestrial organisms in the greenhouse climates of the Cretaceous relied on marine resources to supplement their diets in a similar way that modern organisms do," said first author Dr. Clayton Forster, a geologist at the University of Arkansas. "We can identify that marine resources are passed along the food chain and incorporated in the minerals of bones and teeth of dinosaurs, crocodiles, turtles, and fish."

Mysterious Chemical Clues in Dinosaur Teeth

The discovery helps explain a longstanding mystery involving the chemical composition of dinosaur teeth.

Plants contain two forms of carbon known as isotopes: 'light' (C-12) and 'heavy' (C-13). Scientists can measure the relative amounts of these isotopes, expressed as δ13C, to identify a chemical fingerprint that passes from food into the animals that consume it.

As animals eat, this carbon signature becomes incorporated into their tooth enamel. The δ13C value in enamel is typically higher than that of the food consumed, with living animals generally showing an increase of between 11 and 13 parts per thousand.

However, previous measurements of dinosaur teeth have consistently revealed unusually high values. These readings also exceed what scientists would expect from animals that ate only plants growing on land, which generally have lower δ13C values than most marine plants.

One possible explanation is that dinosaurs, or the animals they consumed, were obtaining some of their nutrients from the ocean.

"By determining the carbon isotope composition of dinosaur, fish, and crocodile tooth enamel, we can determine what their primary dietary source was and if they were different between regions," explained Forster.

Fossils Reveal a Prehistoric Ocean Food Source

To investigate, researchers examined fossils from (once) coastal locations bordering the Western Interior Seaway and the ancient coastline of the Gulf of Mexico. Around 100 million years ago, the Western Interior Seaway was an enormous inland sea that divided North America into two separate landmasses.

The team also analyzed fossils from locations farther inland, allowing them to compare animals that lived near the ocean with those that occupied landlocked environments.

The fossil deposits formed during two intervals of the Cretaceous Period: the early Albian (around 113-107 million years ago) and the early Cenomanian (approximately 100-96 million years ago).

Researchers used powdered fossil material to measure carbon isotope signatures from both periods. They also determined the latitudes where the animals had lived to investigate whether geography influenced the results.

A clear pattern emerged. Fossils from coastal environments consistently contained higher δ13C values than those from the inland formation. Remarkably, the coastal signatures remained similar across different locations, regardless of latitude or geological age.

These findings provide the first evidence of marine subsidization in prehistoric ecosystems, indicating that nutrients originating in the ocean were entering food chains on land millions of years ago.

Seaweed May Have Been on the Dinosaur Menu

The researchers next considered what ocean food source could explain the widespread chemical signatures.

"Coastal-dwelling organisms must have eaten some kind of organic matter from the ocean, or prey that had done so. This pattern is shared from fish to megaherbivores and indicates that the extra carbon source must have been low in the food-chain to affect both aquatic and terrestrial animals," Forster explained.

For the same chemical pattern to appear in such a wide variety of animals, the marine food source would likely have entered the food chain near its base. It also needed to be something that existed along coastlines but was absent farther inland, while remaining available for millions of years.

Seaweed emerged as the most likely explanation.

"Few organisms meet these criteria besides marine macroalgae or macrophytes - seaweeds," said Forster. "Given the almost ubiquitous behavior of large coastal herbivores today to supplement their diet with seaweeds, it's likely that most of the sampled herbivorous dinosaurs were no different."

Modern plant-eating animals living near coastlines often consume seaweed to supplement their diets. The fossil evidence suggests that many herbivorous dinosaurs may have behaved similarly, with marine nutrients also passing to other animals through the food chain.

Not Every Dinosaur Had a Taste for the Sea

Despite the widespread evidence of marine nutrients in coastal food webs, the researchers found that not every dinosaur took advantage of these resources.

One notable exception was Tenontosaurus tilletti, a large plant-eating dinosaur whose fossils have been discovered at numerous locations dating to the Cretaceous Period.

Its tooth enamel contained δ13C values comparable to those of modern animals that feed on plants growing on land. This suggests that Tenontosaurus tilletti did not rely on marine food sources, even though other dinosaurs apparently did.

The difference also strengthens the researchers' interpretation of the fossil evidence. If geological processes occurring after death had altered the carbon signatures in dinosaur teeth, the same unusual values would be expected more broadly. Instead, the variation between species suggests that the elevated readings reflect genuine differences in diet.

An Ancient Connection Between Land and Ocean

Although the findings provide strong evidence that marine resources supported the coastal ecosystems examined, important questions remain.

The available fossils do not include specimens from polar or equatorial regions during the early Albian and early Cenomanian. As a result, scientists cannot yet determine how widespread this feeding behavior was across different latitudes.

Additional studies will also be needed to establish whether similar relationships existed during other geological periods, including the earlier Jurassic Period and the later early Cenozoic Era.

Beyond revealing a surprising possibility about what dinosaurs ate, the discovery highlights how closely life on land has been connected to the ocean throughout Earth's history.

"Our study emphasizes the connections between terrestrial and marine ecosystems," concluded Forster. "They are deeply intertwined and have been for hundreds of millions of years. It highlights the importance of environmental linkages across time and space and protecting them where they exist today."
