For Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, one of the hardest parts of traveling to the moon happened before he even left Earth.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Former NASA astronaut Victor Glover has flown in combat, performed four spacewalks and strapped himself to the top of rockets launching into space. But before embarking on his historic Artemis II journey around the moon, he faced something even more difficult: a conversation with his four daughters.

Speaking alongside former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Canary Islands, on Oct. 18, Glover opened up about the challenges of preparing his family for his riskiest mission yet.

"This is maybe the greatest challenge of my astronaut career," Glover said.

Glover joined NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen aboard NASA's Artemis II mission, which launched on April 1, 2026, marking humanity's first crewed journey to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972.

But preparing for the historic journey wasn't just about mastering the spacecraft and executing the mission successfully. It also meant making sure his family was ready for what lay ahead.

When Glover first traveled to space aboard SpaceX's Crew-1 mission in 2020, his children were much younger and he and his wife, Dionna, made a conscious effort to prepare them for his time in space.

"We decided, as a parental unit, Dionna and I, that we were going to put as much effort into making sure our family was ready as NASA was putting into making sure I was ready to be a crew member," Glover explained.

The family visited NASA's Kennedy Space Center, toured the launch pad and crew quarters and even planned when Glover would call home from the International Space Station. But by the time Artemis II came around, things were different. All four of his daughters were now adults, and preparing them for his journey around the moon meant discussing the mission's risks, including the possibility that he might not return home.

Glover recalled his wife telling him something he described as maybe the scariest thing he'd ever heard.

"You should have this talk with our daughters."

And although he knew she was right, it wasn't an easy conversation to have.

"We did, and it did not go well in my opinion," Glover admitted. "Well, it's not about going well. The talk needed to be done, just because it's hard."

The following day, Glover sent his daughters and wife a poem, Live Your Life, by Chief Tecumseh.

The poem helped Glover express something he had struggled to put into words during their conversation: why he believed the risks of traveling to the moon were worth taking.

"It was a very tough conversation, but they understood that I know this is risky. I wasn't just telling them Dad's risking his life. There's a real point to this and there's a reason to take this risk," Glover explained. "This poem helped me to say it in a way that I didn't have words for."

After traveling around the moon and returning safely to Earth, one moment stood out above all others. When we asked Glover in a separate interview at Starmus on Oct. 20, which moment from Artemis II he would most like to relive, he answered immediately.

"It's the true, ultimate mission accomplishment. Just 'we did it.' We survived. My family is relieved, and there's just nothing like it," Glover explained. "There's nothing like coming home. There's nothing like returning to Earth."

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#708. ‘The Body’ Breakout Geena Meszaros on Finding Empathy for Lisbeth and “Life-Altering” Female Friendships

The actress stars as the complicated Lisbeth in Netflix's new queer Catholic coming-of-age psycho thriller.

Actress Geena Meszaros has been galavanting around Hollywood the last few weeks, arm-in-arm with her fellow young actresses from The Body. But a month ago, she was back home in Canada, fresh off some October snow, finding herself in limbo.

Meszaros has been patiently waiting for the Netflix coming-of-age series centered around the dance team at a Catholic school to come out since it wrapped filming earlier this year after six months of shooting. In the week since it’s landed on the streamer, the internet, and the Hollywood party crowds, can’t get enough of the show’s talented gang of young actresses. “I don’t think I was even submitted for it,” she tells The Hollywood Reporter of how she came to join the project. Related Stories TV Netflix Renews Japanese Crime Hit 'Tokyo Swindlers' for Season 2 TV Nikki Glaser Signs Deal With Newly Created Netflix Is a Joke Studios

“Two months before they started filming, I got an email from my agent that one of the producers reached out and asked me to send in a tape,” Meszaros continues. The actress plays Lisbeth, an outsider who joins the Lions dance team and develops a complicated relationship with Kristina Bogic’s Anya.

“All I knew about it was the synopsis, the vague character description and the three scenes that I was given. But that was enough to make me obsessed.”

The actress eventually got a callback and did a few chemistry reads. By that point, she was supposed to have been sent the first three episodes but she hadn’t been. “I didn’t even know how lucky I was,” she says. “I feel like the gods were looking down upon me, and it’s just ended up being the biggest dream role I could dream up.”

Meszaros doesn’t have a moment she can point to when she realized she wanted to be an actor. “I honestly remember it as more of a knowing. I was like, ‘That is what I’m going to do,'” she says. The actress was fascinated by child actors growing up.

“I was just seeing the attention my parents were getting from them. I don’t know, there’s probably something to unpack there,” she says. “It’s intuitive for me. I live most things pretty intuitively, and acting feels like an intuitive thing that I enjoy and comes naturally to me.”

The tone of the show is so unique and needed right now. What was it like being a part of a project that felt different?

I actually have not processed how just absolutely lucky I am. It’s flawless to me. I am always hoping that something that really intrigues me, that I don’t know what’s going to happen, is going to come along. It’s so rare. It’s so hard to get those backed. It’s truly a blessing.

What were the dance rehearsals like for this?

They were so much fun. It was amazing to be able to build those relationships before filming, even though I guess my character’s not everyone’s best friend. Our choreographer, Ryan Heffington, is incredible. It was an honor just to work with him. We were so sore. It was long days, and then halfway through, they realized I didn’t really need to know the dance, but I did learn it anyway. So I got to sit on the side and have FOMO, which was very Lisbeth for me.

You were getting into character. What was it like finding Lisbeth? I imagine, as an actor, a character like this is exciting for you. What did you hone in on first?

When I auditioned, not really knowing anything, I immediately read it as hilarious. I guess not many people did that. I just found it so inspiring to play and have fun with it, so I wanted to make sure I still brought that into it after I learned more about her. On top of that, the most important thing for me was having empathy for her and really understanding why she does everything that she does. Having a certain level of respect for her because she is really so intelligent and so quick to use things to her advantage. I found that impressive. I found that really admirable, honestly, for a not so admirable human.

Why do you think that’s so important for you to find empathy for her?

If I were to just play her scary and manipulative — although I know she does come across as maybe manipulative… I just think it’s far more interesting to watch [by not doing that]. Having empathy for a character like that feels important. As far as acting goes, it’s not the most noble crusade. That feels like something I can do that’s maybe helpful to someone. Rather than manipulative, she’s really more of an opportunist, I think. I don’t think she planted the seed. She’s maybe just watering it. That’s A, more fun, B, more real. Because no one is truly good or bad entirely.

How does this role in particular fit into where you are trying to see yourself as an actor?

This is a question that has never been asked to me until recently, and I spent so long trying not to think of where I wanted to be that it’s like…

Yeah. I really just trust that the things that are meant for me are going to find me, but I love Mia Goth, which is weird because I don’t so much love watching horror, but to play it feels very cathartic, I think. Anything with some grit, anything that’s original, I’m happy to do.

You’re getting to work with several actors at a very similar point in their career as you’re at. What as it been like to do this with the whole group?

That’s a big part of why this big group of girls genuinely gets along, which is a miracle. We were all just so grateful to be there all the way through it, and we all wanted to give it our all. I think that’s it. We were just all so in awe that we were even in the room that we were in.

Do you have a most memorable experience from shooting it?

The whole thing is a giant blur of chaos and just love and hanging out with all of my new best friends. I’ve never ever been part of a giant girl friend group, and that’s just honestly life-altering for me. It’s so lovely. I get how Lisbeth feels because it really is so empowering to be part of a group. I want to squeeze them all. They’re all perfect.

#707. ‘I had felt overconfident’: senior scientists reveal mistakes that aided discovery

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Meghie Rodrigues is a science and climate journalist in Paraná, Brazil.

Physicist Peter Shawhan and his team perfected not finding gravitational waves at the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) facility in Livingston, Louisiana — until they did. Credit: Igor Andreoni/Peter Shawhan

To err is human, science endeavours included. Accounts of missteps in the laboratory or field abound among early-career researchers, as do tales of what they learnt from them. But senior scientists make mistakes, too — and not just early in their careers.

Sometimes, reaching a dead end was the only way around a problem. Other times, graduate students saved their advisers from throwing away ‘wrong’ data. Senior scientists also know the dangers of overthinking and how it can lead to experimental paralysis. “Every year, I devote a meeting with students and postdocs to discuss failures and how errors of judgement or methods are part of academic life,” says Catherine Badgley, a palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. “I hope this helps them to see they can learn from mistakes rather than be devastated by them.”

Nature’s careers team spoke to Badgley and four other senior scientists to hear about their ‘failures’ and the lessons they took from them.

Physicist at the University of Maryland in College Park and a deputy spokesperson for the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) scientific collaboration.

For the past 26 years, I have been searching for gravitational waves with LIGO, which has a gravitational-wave observatory in Livingston, Louisiana. These waves are echoes of massive events such as the merging of black holes or the collision of neutron stars. They produce ripples in space-time and, by the time these tiny ripples reach Earth, they are so faint that scientists need extra help to ‘hear’ them, because they are extremely hard to detect by just using light, or telescopes, to see them. For example, observations of a collision of two neutron stars with telescopes has revealed the presence of gold and platinum atoms, solving a long-standing question: what is the origin of about half of all elements heavier than iron? The detection of such an event with LIGO would get us even more information.

In the first tests of LIGO, the team found nothing. Later, with improved detectors, we still found nothing.

In fact, we got very good at reporting nothing. We became experienced with knowing what we could rule out. By the time we made our first wave detection, in 2015, a finding that earned LIGO founders a physics Nobel in 2017, we had published about 100 papers reporting null results.

One such null case was in 2010. We were completing a science run, in which data are collected for a set period of time, and had a candidate for a striking event — it looked like we’d finally got there. But we knew it might be a ‘blind injection’, which is when a false signal is inserted into a data set by authorized colleagues to test our analyses.

We finished the analysis, drafted the paper and then asked the LIGO director to open a sealed envelope to tell us whether this was a real event or not. It wasn’t, but the exercise showed a real problem: the sky location our analysis recovered didn’t match the signal’s known location. Two of the detector’s mirrors had moved in the wrong direction. We found the glitch in about a day. This showed we could efficiently self-correct when detecting a real sign — which happened five years later.

I tell my students that scientists make lots of mistakes. We’re careful with cross-checks and analyse results carefully, so we catch almost all of them. Some are caught in minutes, some in days and some take more work. This one, because we’d built a test designed to assess itself, took about a day. That’s really the goal: not avoiding mistakes, but rather building enough ways to catch them quickly. Knowing what it means to find nothing is important; it’s a real scientific skill.

Chemist Omar Yaghi (second row, fifth from right), with his team at Tsinghua University in Beijing, says that professors can learn important lessons from their students if they listen to them.Credit: Yaghi Group Photo

Chemist at Tsinghua University in Beijing and a co-recipient of the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work with metal–organic frameworks.

Back in the 1990s, I was an assistant professor at Arizona State University in Tempe. My team had begun research trying to make inorganic porous materials. These are solid materials with a network of tiny, connected pores that act like molecular sponges to trap molecules, such as wastewater contaminants and toxic gases, on their surfaces. We were successful: we had a paper1 published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society and, later, in Science2.

Then a doctoral student came looking to join my lab. She didn’t sound very confident, her English was not so good and it wasn’t the right time of year to look for a PhD adviser. I made up some reason not to take her. But she kept coming back and was adamant about working with me.

So I accepted her into my lab group, and she started working on metal–organic compounds, another type of porous material. I felt that this was a waste of time: researchers had known about these structures since the 1950s, but nothing useful had resulted from them. Once you emptied their solvent-filled pores to trap other molecules, such as gases, they collapsed and became useless. I used to call them sculptures: they had beauty, but no function.

She kept at it, and I held onto my scepticism. After a year, we sat down to discuss her results. That was when I realized that there was an opportunity there: we could make robust metal–organic compounds, after all.

Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are also materials full of tiny pores. But what makes them particularly interesting is that scientists can adjust the size and shape of those pores, as well as the chemical properties inside them. This makes MOFs more tunable than inorganic porous materials such as zeolites and much better at trapping some gases. Some MOFs can drive chemical reactions, some conduct electricity and some are stable enough to be reused.

My student found strong chemical bindings that gave stability to early versions of these structures and, within a very short period, our findings were published in Nature3. It had worked.

Decades later, I met with my former student, and she told me that she had been struggling back then and wanted to try her luck with me, a new professor at the time, because no one else would take her in.

I think science is the greatest equalizer. One discovery can take you from humble beginnings, as it did for us, and propel you to the top of your profession.

I had an opinion about an area of research and didn’t listen to my student, and, to that student’s credit, she persisted. To my credit, I changed my thinking. Neither the student nor the professor can afford to do science without the other.

Plant geneticist Chris Martine’s misidentified sample led to the identification of a new species of bush tomato plant in northern Australia. Credit: Jason Cantley

Plant geneticist at Bucknell University in Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, and president of the Botanical Society of America.

I’ve studied Australia’s bush tomatoes for about 25 years. My team was the first to describe Solanum ossicruentum, nicknamed the blood bone tomato because it seems to bleed when cut open. It got us some press coverage and was a big deal for our laboratory in 20164.

In 2017, Angela McDonnell, a postdoc, joined us. We started a big genetics project to build an evolutionary tree to understand the family history of the bush tomatoes we had been studying for years. We had two samples of S. ossicruentum from two locations: the Tanami Desert and the Keep River National Park, both in northern Australia. When the results of testing came back, genomic differences landed them in totally different places on the evolutionary tree of the group.

In my mind, there was no way it was possible. I’d identified the specimens myself. I assumed we’d mislabelled something. I asked Angela to check everything carefully, but she was certain that wasn’t the case. To me it didn’t add up — I came close to saying, “let’s just pull the misplaced one and call it an error”.

Two years ago, while looking through the folders of S. ossicruentum specimens at the Northern Territory Herbarium in Palmerston, Australia, I noticed some that had strange dots on the backs of their leaves. At first, I thought it was mildew, but then I wondered whether these dots were extrafloral nectaries, or nectar-producing glands found outside the plant’s flower. Then I realized the plants with such dots were mostly from one part of Australia, the northern edge of the Tanami Desert — exactly where I was heading next.

When I got there, plants with these little dots were dripping with nectar with ants harvesting it, an interaction I hadn’t seen to this level before. I checked whether Angela’s big phylogeny project had anything from that region, and there it was — the misplaced plant. The two samples of what I thought were S. ossicruentum belonged in two different places on the evolutionary tree because they were two different species. Indeed, that initial sample’s evolutionary tree placement was the best evidence for the new species that we later described: Solanum nectarifolium5. My first thought was to thank Angela for not pulling that specimen out of our analysis. I was honestly thrilled.

Before that, I had felt overconfident in what I knew, and Angela was certain that this was a carefully curated data set and a rigorously achieved genetic result. As I’ve become more senior, I’ve become more comfortable with uncertainty: when something doesn’t fit our preconceived ideas, that’s an interesting result — that’s how you find more new things.

Now I realize how important it is for people who are more junior than myself to speak up and share their ideas, especially when they run counter to convention. If we look back at the history of science, that’s the only way we’ve progressed.

Palaeontologist Catherine Badgley says that a key skill for scientists is knowing when to stop pursuing a good idea that simply isn’t working. Credit: David Bay

Palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor.

In the 1990s, I was an associate research scientist in the University of Michigan’s Museum of Paleontology. Serge Legendre, a colleague who was then at the University of Montpellier in France, showed me a new way, at the time, of explaining body-size distributions in fossils of extinct mammalian species. He used cenograms — a graphical technique that ranks mammalian species in a community by body size.

In well-watered ecosystems, there was a fairly continuous line: all species were closely spaced in size. But habitats with long dry seasons had a big gap in the middle where medium-sized mammals would be — an interesting mystery. Legendre found that many animals in that size range are fruit-eaters, and fruit isn’t available in arid or very cold environments all year long. If the theory was correct, we might be able to infer past climate from the sizes of mammals in fossil communities.

I had a lot of climate data for mammal locations worldwide, so the two of us, as well as palaeontologist Philip Gingerich, who was then also at the University of Michigan, decided to build a much larger database of locations and add climate variables. We wanted to determine whether climate variables could predict the size gap we saw. I was excited enough that I wrote it up as a book proposal and received a contract from the University of Chicago Press.

But the more data that we collected, the fuzzier the picture became. After more than a year, I had written four chapters. But I had to admit we had fewer results than when we started.

I knew the data weren’t flawed because I had used this enormous mammalian fossil database successfully for other research projects. For example, undergraduate students used it to show that the length of the growing season, as a climate variable, could be used to predict the number of fruit- and plant-eating species at a given time.

I eventually realized that each continent has its own evolutionary history and its own climatic circumstances — no one is exactly like another. Our largest data sets, from Africa and North America, have almost completely non-overlapping climates, so one was never going to be a good model for predicting the other.

The record highlights the enormous distances involved in deep-space exploration.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After nearly 50 years traveling through space, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a milestone no human-made object has reached before: a distance of one light-day from Earth.

This milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (1016:07 GMT) — highlights the immense distances Voyager 1 has traveled and the challenges of communicating with spacecraft operating in the outer reaches of the solar system and beyond.

Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours. Light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second, meaning one light-day is roughly 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), according to a statement from NASA.

Although the term light-day might sound like a measurement of time, it is actually a unit of distance, much like a light-year. Astronomers use light-based measurements because conventional miles and kilometers become increasingly difficult to comprehend when describing the enormous distances between objects in space.

For perspective on how far Voyager 1 has travelled, sunlight takes about eight minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, meaning our planet is approximately 8.3 light-minutes from the sun. Radio signals traveling between Earth and Mars can take anywhere from three to 22 minutes, depending on the planets' positions in their orbits, according to the statement.

By comparison, when Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth, a radio signal sent from the probe will take a full 24 hours to reach mission controllers on Earth, and a command transmitted from Earth will take another 24 hours to reach the spacecraft.

The communication delay affects how engineers operate spacecraft at such distances. Unlike spacecraft operating closer to Earth, which can receive commands and return data with relatively little delay, communicating with Voyager 1 requires mission controllers to account for the extended signal travel time when planning spacecraft operations, troubleshooting technical issues and evaluating the results of commands sent to the probe.

Voyager 1 has been traveling away from Earth since its launch on Sept. 5, 1977. Now cruising through interstellar space at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 kph), the spacecraft has spent more than 49 years covering the distance that light can cross in a single day.

Even at that speed, Voyager 1 is moving relatively slowly compared with light itself. Its twin, Voyager 2, which launched in 1977 on a different trajectory, is expected to reach the same one-light-day milestone in November 2035.

As Voyager 1 and, eventually, Voyager 2 continue their journeys through interstellar space, their growing distances from Earth offer a measure of both the reach of human exploration and the communication challenges that come with sending spacecraft ever farther into the cosmos.

Samantha Mathewson joined Space.com as an intern in the summer of 2016. She received a B.A. in Journalism and Environmental Science at the University of New Haven, in Connecticut. Previously, her work has been published in Nature World News. When not writing or reading about science, Samantha enjoys traveling to new places and taking photos! You can follow her on Twitter @Sam_Ashley13.

#705. Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns

The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 exceptionally ancient quasars, including two that have set new records as the earliest ever observed. These brilliant galactic centers, powered by enormous black holes, were already radiating as much light as a trillion Suns when the Universe was only 670 million years old, about 5% of its present age.

Quasars are among the brightest objects in the cosmos. They appear during a relatively short period in a galaxy's history when huge quantities of gas and other material spiral toward its central supermassive black hole. This process releases extraordinary amounts of energy, causing the galaxy's core to shine hundreds or even thousands of times more brightly than the rest of the galaxy combined.

Astronomers have spent decades searching for quasars from the Universe's earliest years because they offer valuable clues about the formation of the first galaxies and supermassive black holes. Finding them, however, is extremely challenging. Few galaxies had grown large enough to host such objects at that early stage, and the light reaching us today is incredibly faint. These distant sources can also be difficult to distinguish from stars much closer to Earth.

Launched in 2023, Euclid is transforming that search. Its ability to survey enormous regions of the sky and detect faint objects has already produced an unprecedented collection of 31 quasars from the early Universe, including some dating back to when the cosmos was just 5% of its current age.

"These early quasars date back to the Universe's infancy," says Daming Yang of Leiden University in the Netherlands, lead author of the Euclid discovery paper. "By finding and studying them, we can better understand how these enormous systems formed and grew so quickly - one of the greatest mysteries in astrophysics."

Euclid Reveals a Hidden Population of Ancient Quasars

Until now, astronomers had identified only a small fraction of the quasars that existed during the Universe's earliest period. Most known examples were exceptionally luminous objects that stood out because they were easier to detect. This limited sample made it difficult to understand the broader population and how these powerful systems developed.

Euclid is changing that picture by identifying not only the brightest quasars but also much fainter examples that previous searches struggled to find. Its discoveries are providing scientists with a far more representative view of the ancient quasar population, opening the door to more detailed studies of these early cosmic objects.

"Euclid is a true game-changer," adds Daming. "Before, we could only find a handful of the very brightest ancient quasars, but Euclid lets us search far more efficiently across huge areas of sky to capture much fainter light. It's a unique tool for quasar hunting."

Among the 31 newly identified quasars, 12 have a redshift of 7 or greater. Redshift describes how light is stretched as the Universe expands and helps astronomers determine how far away an object is and how far back in cosmic history its light originated. A redshift of at least 7 places these quasars within the Universe's first 770 million years.

Two Record-Breaking Quasars From Cosmic Dawn

Two objects stand out as particularly extraordinary. The most ancient, EUCL J172902.75+641018.1, has a redshift of 7.77, while EUCL J125308.55+705432.3 has a redshift of 7.69. Both are located just over 13 billion light-years from Earth and were already shining within the first 670 million years of cosmic history.

These discoveries establish new records for the earliest known quasars. The previous record belonged to an object discovered in 2021, which has a redshift of 7.64.

"This finding more than doubles the number of quasars we know of that are so ancient," says Antonio La Marca, an ESA Research Fellow in the Euclid team.

The pace of discovery is especially remarkable. Astronomers needed more than a decade to identify roughly the first 10 quasars with redshifts of 7 or higher. Euclid has already surpassed that number in just one year, demonstrating how dramatically the telescope is accelerating research into the early Universe.

"The Euclid team has taken a true 'census' of quasars at the dawn of the Universe for the first time," adds Antonio. "It's a big step towards understanding these fascinating objects on a more fundamental level."

Ancient Black Holes Reveal Clues About the First Galaxies

One of the newly discovered objects is already offering additional insight into conditions during the Universe's infancy. Silvia Belladitta and colleagues recently conducted a more detailed investigation of the second most ancient quasar identified by Daming and his team.

Their observations revealed that the quasar sits inside a galaxy filled with gas and dust where new stars are forming at a tremendous rate. This provides an important glimpse of the environment surrounding an early supermassive black hole and could help researchers understand how the first massive galaxies evolved alongside the black holes at their centers.

These quasars also belong to a transformative chapter in cosmic history known as the epoch of reionization. During this period, the Universe emerged from a cold, dark state (the 'dark ages') as increasingly energetic radiation heated the surrounding gas and ionized it (split apart by energetic light). This fundamental transition helped establish the conditions that shaped the Universe we observe today.

"Ancient quasars are rare discoveries. They're interesting in themselves, but also time machines that enable us to explore the early Universe and understand how the first generation of galaxies came to be," says ESA Euclid Project Scientist Valeria Pettorino.

How Euclid Is Transforming the Search for Cosmic Giants

Euclid's success comes from a powerful combination of capabilities. The telescope can examine enormous portions of the sky while collecting detailed images and detecting faint infrared light from extremely distant objects. Together, these features make it exceptionally effective at finding rare sources that earlier surveys could easily miss.

"Euclid's capabilities are unrivaled. The telescope combines a large area, depth, sharp imaging, and unique space-based infrared vision in a way that lets us pick out rare, extremely distant objects far more efficiently than before.

"And it's not just the telescope: the data processing is only possible thanks to thousands of Euclid Consortium scientists and engineers working together to deliver scientific discoveries, sifting through enormous datasets to identify rare, distant quasars that we can study further using telescopes on the ground."

All 31 quasars were identified using observations from the Euclid Wide Survey, an ambitious project that will eventually examine more than one-third of the entire sky.

Although Euclid's primary mission is to investigate the dark Universe, its observations are revealing much more. By studying billions of galaxies, the telescope is helping astronomers investigate the Universe's composition, history, evolution, and vast cosmic structure. At the same time, its sweeping survey is uncovering rare ancient quasars that offer a remarkable opportunity to explore how the first galaxies and giant black holes emerged.

As Euclid continues mapping the cosmos, astronomers expect its growing collection of distant quasars to provide new clues about one of astrophysics' most enduring questions: how supermassive black holes became so enormous in such a remarkably short time after the Big Bang.

#704. Elon Musk says SpaceX’s Starship, already the largest rocket on Earth, will get even bigger with next-gen V4 model

"Starship V4 will be ~70m long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," the SpaceX CEO said.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As usual, SpaceX and its founder Elon Musk are thinking big.

The company recovered the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever on Saturday (Nov. 14), plucking it out of the sky with the "chopstick" arms of its Texas launch tower.

It was a huge moment for SpaceX, bringing its vision of full and rapid rocket reuse much closer to reality. But Elon Musk isn't one to dwell on the past or rest on laurels, so he soon outlined an even more ambitious future for Starship.

"Starship V4 will be ~70m [230 feet] long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Sunday evening (Nov. 15). "Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher-thrust V4 engines."

The current version of Starship — the one that launched Friday (Nov. 13) on the vehicle's 15th test flight — is the V3. It's the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing 408 feet (124 m) tall when fully stacked with its Super Heavy first stage and Ship upper stage.

V3's Ship is 171 feet (52 m) tall and features six of SpaceX's Raptor V3 engines. (The similarly reusable Super Heavy V3 booster is powered by 33 Raptors.) So, as Musk noted in his post, the V4 Ship will be quite an upgrade in size and power.

Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon.

Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.

To provide a little perspective about that vehicle's planned dimensions: The V4 Ship will be the same height as a fully stacked Falcon 9, SpaceX's workhorse two-stage rocket, and much broader: Ship is 30 feet (9 m) across, while the Falcon 9's payload fairing is 17.1 feet (5.2 m) wide.

This isn't the first we've heard about a V4 Starship. Back in August 2025, for example, Musk posted a graphic showing Starship's planned progression from the V2 to the V3 to the V4, which he said is expected to debut in 2027.

That slide pegs the future Starship's total height at 466 feet (142 m), 200 feet (61 m) of which would be Ship. But those numbers are out of date, Musk stressed in the post, saying that V4 is "probably closer to 150m height."

So, yeah: If all goes according to plan, the next Starship will be nearly 500 feet tall.

Starship V4 will be ~70m long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load. Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher thrust V4 engines.November 16, 2026

The original Starship Flight 15 mission plan called for a double chopsticks catch, with both Super Heavy and Ship coming back to the launch tower for recovery.

This would have been feasible, as the catches were scheduled a day apart: Super Heavy would land just 6.5 minutes after launch, while Ship would circle Earth for 22.5 hours, and deploy a batch of SpaceX's Starlink V3 internet satellites, before coming home. (Ship ended up delivering the satellites as planned.)

The twofer didn't happen, however; Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday as a result. But that wasn't a huge deal, as SpaceX had already pulled off Super Heavy catches on three previous Starship flights.

The Ship catch was unprecedented, because it's been a taller order. Ship returns to Earth from orbit, so it comes in faster and hotter. SpaceX hadn't even tried the maneuver before Flight 15, so executing it was a very big deal.

"That was the missing link," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during the company's Ship-landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#703. Germany's 2027 budget: A record €561 billion and a mountain of debt

The 2027 federal budget proposal has finally been hammered out and is set for a vote in parliament. What are the government's policy priorities in defense, infrastructure, the economy and social spending?

It was 5:55 a.m. on Friday when the Bundestag's Budget Committee concluded its final session.

Following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget. The opposition parties — the environmentalist Greens, the socialist Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — voted against it. With that, the way is now clear for the final vote in the Bundestag on November 27.

Reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching. Next year, the federal government plans to spend around €561 billion ($620 billion).

But here's the problem: it won't collect nearly enough revenue to cover these expenses. With a shortfall of €123 billion, borrowing will be needed to bridge the gap.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But that's not the only problem. On top of all this debt, Germany also has loans for defense spending and for the renovation of the dilapidated infrastructure. Approved by the Bundestag in 2025, these special funds are set to be in place for multiple years.

If the new debt for 2027 is factored in, the total borrowing amounts to over €210 billion. This is the second-highest level of borrowing in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany. The only time Germany borrowed more was during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, when borrowing reached €215.4 billion.

This development has drawn sharp criticism from opposition parties. Green Party lawmaker Sebastian Schäfer and his colleague Dietmar Bartsch of the Left Party called it a "gigantic mountain of debt," an "untrustworthy" budget, "irresponsible" policies at the expense of future generations and a lack of future prospects.

To understand the reasons behind the growing debt, one has to look beyond the numbers. Every federal budget is a snapshot of the priorities set by a government and a country — in terms of the economy, social issues, security and geopolitics.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For 2027, that story continues to be one of crises and wars. While Russia's war against Ukraine is driving up defense spending, the faltering economy is also demanding new investments. At the same time, Germany's population is aging rapidly, which is driving up social spending.

What's more, the crumbling infrastructure must be repaired and modernized, and the energy transition is costing billions. And more than half of all this debt is going toward security and defense.

Russia's war against Ukraine will enter its sixth year in 2027. As of the end of June, the federal government estimated its overall support for Ukraine to have reached approximately €100 billion. In response to a request from the AfD in the Bundestag, the government stated: "The federal government will continue to provide Ukraine with political, financial, humanitarian, civil and military support for as long as necessary."

The rearmament of the Bundeswehr and spending on NATO are also putting massive pressure on the budget. The defense budget is set to grow to just under €110 billion in 2027, an increase of around €27 billion compared to last year. Added to this are expenditures from the Bundeswehr's special fund.

Nevertheless, by far the largest single budget item comes from the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is set to grow to over €200 billion. There are plans for cost-cutting measures, for example, in basic income support for job seekers. But the costs of old-age pension benefits continue to rise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

People born in the 1960s have begun to retire. Back then, more than 1 million children were born each year. But birth rates nearly halved in the early 1970s and have continued to decline since then. As a result, there will be an increasing number of retirees and a decreasing number of working-age individuals in the coming years.

The pension funds cannot be financed by the pension contributions of this dwindling workforce and have to be subsidized by the government. Already, contributions to the pension insurance system — which are split equally between employees and employers — will have to be increased. They are expected to rise to just under 20% of gross salary.

The Federal Employment Agency, too, has long been unable to make ends meet on contributions alone. In 2027, subsidies of more than €8 billion from the federal budget are planned.

Anyone comparing Germany's current budget situation with that of past years will be rubbing their eyes in disbelief. It wasn't that long ago that Germany was considered a model of fiscal discipline. Between 2014 and 2019, the federal budget managed to avoid taking on new debt for six consecutive years. In some years, there was even money left over.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But the era of "balanced budgets" came to an abrupt end with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. However, today Germany is still enjoying the benefits of those years of fiscal stability. Compared to other countries, Germany is still in relatively good shape.

The key indicator is not the amount of debt along but the debt-to-GDP ratio. It indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output.

At the end of 2025, it stood at 63.5% for Germany. France, on the other hand, stands at over 110% and Italy at about 135% to 140%, while the US is well above 100%. However, in its latest fall report, the German Council of Economic Experts warned that Germany could be heading down a dangerous path. If debt continues to rise at this rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio could climb to 100% by 2040.

This would also put Germany's creditworthiness on the financial markets at risk. Germany is the only country among the seven leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) that still holds a triple-A (AAA) rating. This is the highest possible credit rating on the financial markets. It signals to investors that the risk of default on German government bonds is extremely low.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This also means that interest rates on new loans are not set as high. This is an important point, as interest payments place an increasing burden on the federal budget each year. By 2027, approximately €42 billion in interest payments are expected to be due.

At the end of November, the Bundestag will hold its final debate on the draft budget. Should changes be expected by then? There is disagreement within the government over whether a reduction in the electricity tax might still be possible.

The prospect of such a reduction had been raised by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. On Friday, during a European leaders summit in Dublin, he reiterated: "I expect that we will discuss this again next Tuesday in the coalition committee, and I remain committed to my goal of lowering the electricity tax to the European minimum — in full — starting next year."

#702. Harrison Ford Kisses Calista Flockhart On Stage As Couple Receives Their First Joint Award

Flockhart revealed the reason they said yes to the honor before joking that her other half didn't need convincing: "Between you and me, Harrison complains that he doesn't get enough attention."

When Women’s Guild Cedars-Sinai reached out to ask Harrison Ford and Calista Flockhart if they would join forces to accept a Hollywood Icon Award at the Stardust Ball, the organization got a quick answer.

“We didn’t hesitate. We said yes. We said yes, yes, yes,” Flockhart revealed while standing next to her husband on a ballroom stage inside at Beverly Wilshire, A Four Seasons Hotel on Wednesday night. “And I promise you, it was not because we wanted an award. Well, actually maybe [Harrison] did. Between you and me, Harrison complains that he doesn’t get enough attention. But really, it’s true. I’m not joking.” Related Stories Lifestyle Harrison Ford Joins Greg Berlanti, Goldie Hawn and Melissa McCarthy as Paley Gala Honorees Business Byron Allen Sells His Stake in Starz

Judging by the look on Ford’s face, it was hard to tell if Flockhart was teasing. Either way, they received a loads of attention as the night’s marquee honorees alongside media mogul Byron Allen, who received a humanitarian award for his philanthropic work. Normally a private couple, Ford and Flockhart seemed to enjoy the moment as they beamed with joy and even stopped to share a kiss in front of the capacity crowd. The night’s program also featured host Sheryl Underwood and auctioneer Billy Harris with a performance by Jett Stanfield, Brandon Keith Rogers, A.J. Mendoza and Josh Black of the Company Men.

Also making a big appearance was Ford’s Star Wars colleague Mark Hamill, who offered a brief tribute to his longtime franchise pal. Attention aside, the night was notable as it marked Ford and Flockhart’s first joint award as a couple. They’ve been in lock step on plenty of red carpets over the course of their decades-long romance but hadn’t shared a stage until Wednesday evening. The Stardust Ball proved to be an ideal situation as they both have ties to and admiration for Cedars-Sinai. But it also offered a chance to pay respects to close friends like physicians Bruce Gewertz and Randy Sherman.

The former, a nationally known vascular surgeon, served as a technical advisor on Ford’s 1993 thriller The Fugitive, while the latter was an internationally renowned surgeon who helped build plastic surgery programs in Los Angeles while traveling the world treating children with complex deformities. Sherman, who served as vice chair in the surgery department and director plastic surgery at Cedars-Sinai, died July 18, 2023, in an air traffic accident in Santa Fe, New Mexico.

Gewertz was in the ballroom and took the stage to offer a tribute. He recalled how he helped The Fugitive’s scribes nail “the medical part of the plot” while training Ford to look as much like a vascular surgeon as possible in the operating room. “I shrewdly negotiated a very rich compensation package with Warner Brothers: Harrison would tuck my kids in at night, and somehow, despite having absolutely no business being in front of a camera, I was included in a small part in the movie, which for the past 33 years has provided me with a steady income every couple of months — after taxes — of about $20,” explained Gewertz.

Beyond spending money, the real reward “the opportunity to get to know Harrison Ford, a man who is “even more impressive than the legendary characters he has created,” Gewertz continued. He then went on to praise Ford’s environmental activism as a long-serving board member of Conservation International and for sticking his neck out on behalf of forests, oceans and fragile ecosystems. Gewertz praised Flockhart’s philanthropic endeavors too as she’s been of service to “causes involving women, children, health and social issues” through work with For Goodness Sakes, Peace Over Violence and the Violence Intervention Program.

Gewertz also revealed that as a couple, they “generously supported” an educational and research fund in honor of Sherman. “Their inspirational philanthropy allows us to pursue discoveries that may change medicines for generations to come, to care for patients who have nowhere else to turn, and most importantly, to honor Randy’s life and legacy,” he said.

In accepting, Ford went first with his comments following a standing ovation. “I’m genuinely touched by what you said,” the actor said to Gewertz, “although I don’t think anyone should hear that many exceedingly kind things about themselves, it feels like a eulogy at my age.”

The quip landed to plenty of laughs, then Ford turned his attention to Sherman by praising his tireless work on behalf of Operation Smile as he flew all over the world to help “rebuild the faces” of children suffering from cleft palates.

For many years on behalf of Operation Smile, Randy tirelessly traveled the world, rebuilding the faces of children suffering from cleft lips and cleft palates. “When a devastating earthquake hit Haiti in 2010, Randy quickly put together a mission for us in support of Operation Smile. We flew my Cessna Caravan from here to Miami where we picked up a plane load of doctors, technicians, medical equipment and supplies for a remote community in the mountains of Haiti,” recalled Ford. “We landed in the middle of town in a field and walked into a hospital that had two overcome doctors, no usable operating room, no supplies, and many patients in terrible, desperate need. I will never forget watching Randy and the others get to work while I hid my tears at what I was seeing.”

Ford continued: “Randy flew many such missions over many, many years. I went back to telling stories and making faces for a living. Years later, as soon as he was able, Bruce brought Randy to Cedars-Sinai and put him in charge of plastic surgery. Through his expertise in reconstructive and microsurgery, Randy helped complex patients with previously untreatable birthdays and traumatic physical injuries. Randy Sherman personified the level of care and caring found at Cedars-Sinai.”

Ford then tossed to Flockhart, who assumed position in front of the microphone to deliver her own remarks. But first, another joke: “It is a rare occasion when I agree with anything that Harrison says, but I do. Tonight, I agree. I enthusiastically agree. You should enjoy it [Harrison].”

The veteran actress paid her respects to the Women’s Guild, and then closed her remarks by personally thanking the staff at Cedars-Sinai for “the incredible care” that her mother received, and for the way they welcomed Flockhart and her only son into the hospital. “They not only took excellent care of him, they took excellent care of me, the very worried mother,” she added. “I also have a personal experience. The amazing [Dr. David Kulber] fixed my hand. Well, actually he fixed my finger. He fixed my special finger. He fixed the most important finger.”

With that, Flockhart raised her middle finger in the air. “True story. I was lucky enough to experience the commitment and the humanity firsthand. And that’s a pun, but it was a good one,” she quipped. “OK, so everyone at Cedars-Sinai to me is an icon of brilliant and compassionate care.”

STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time.

Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase.

It was the first-ever Ship catch, and a huge milestone toward SpaceX's ultimate goal: making Starship completely reusable.

Liftoff occurred from Pad 2 at 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local time) on Friday, against a near cloudless blue sky. Super Heavy is powered by 33 Raptor 3 engines, which provide more than 18 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. And lift off the booster did.

Starship roared off the pad under the power of those Raptors, pulsing visible shockwaves through the plume ejected from the rocket's flame trench.

The first couple minutes of flight went nominally; the vehicle climbed into the sky, gearing up for the hot-staging separation of Super Heavy and Ship — all of which was visible for miles, thanks to the clear Texas skies.

Space.com's images taken from the media’s launch viewing area were shot on a Canon R5 Mark II, with an RF 200-800mm lens that made the sharp pictures of Starship’s liftoff and return possible from almost 4 miles away.

This mirrorless Canon has specs that make it one of the best cameras available right now, with impressive features and functionality, including a 45MP sensor and excellent high-ISO handling.

Check our in-depth Canon R5 Mark II review.

A successful separation occurred at T+2:21 minutes, as Starship soared approximately 40 miles (65 km) overhead. Once disconnected from its booster, Ship increased its thrust and continued onward to space, while Super Heavy, reoriented for its boostback burn and return to Starbase.

That return, however, did not go entirely as planned. Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel alarm and autonomously shifted to an offshore splashdown rather than a catch attempt at Starbase.

Super heavy performed its landing burn above the Gulf of Mexico before cutting its engines for a brief moment and exploding in a giant fireball.

This was an intentional detonation, courtesy of the vehicle's flight termination system.

Ship continued on to low Earth orbit, where it deployed a payload of 26 upgraded Starlink Version 3 satellites. It was the second batch of V3 Starlinks delivered during Starship’s recent flight tests, each of which has added what SpaceX says is the equivalent of 10 Falcon 9 Starlink V2 satellite launches worth of data capacity to its orbital constellation.

Flight 15 was also Starship's second-ever mission to orbit, and its longest so far. Ship spent nearly a full day in orbit, circling Earth a total of 14 times. During its jaunt in space, the spacecraft cleared three separate check points, which allowed SpaceX the opportunity to divert the vehicle for an ocean splashdown if needed, and finally was given the green light to attempt the first-ever Ship tower catch.

At approximately 4:18 p.m. EST (2018 GMT, 3:18 p.m. local time in Texas) on Saturday (Nov. 14), the spacecraft broke through the cloud cover that blanketed the skies above Starbase as onlookers watched its bellyflop plunge toward the ground. Moments after becoming visible, Ship ignited its engines for a flip and burn maneuver, which oriented it upright and swung its trajectory into the tightening grip of the chopstick arms of Starbase's "Mechazilla" launch tower.

After a slight sway back and forth suspended above Earth in Mechazilla's embrace, Ship came to a complete rest, hanging motionless as a historic milestone in SpaceX’s pursuit of fully reusable spaceflight.

It hung there overnight as engineers, and even SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, inspected the spacecraft. Ship was lowered on Sunday (Nov. 15) and transported back to SpaceX's Starbase hanger bay for further checkouts.

SpaceX has not yet said whether Ship 42 will fly again, but its return gives engineers a chance to examine how the spacecraft held up through launch, nearly a day in orbit and atmospheric reentry.

Those findings will help inform upcoming flights as SpaceX ramps up production to continue testing Starship's capabilities.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He has worked the space beat since 2016, covering the evolution of NASA's commercial spaceflight partnerships and crewed missions, planetary science missions, the Artemis program and humanity's return to the moon. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#700. Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize. Researchers at the University of Missouri have found that older adults who follow regular daily schedules tend to experience less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggle to get a good night's sleep.

The findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an important role in physical and mental well-being. By helping the body maintain its natural internal clock, a predictable routine could offer health benefits that extend beyond improved sleep.

The discovery could be especially important for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties. According to the National Council on Aging, roughly half of adults age 60 and older report symptoms of insomnia, a condition that can make it difficult to fall asleep, stay asleep, or get restful sleep.

Daily Routines Linked to Less Pain and Depression

To investigate the relationship between sleep, daily habits, and overall health, Eunjin Tracy, an assistant professor in the College of Education and Human Development at the University of Missouri, examined survey responses from 67 older adults. Among the participants, 37 reported experiencing insomnia.

As researchers expected, those with insomnia generally reported more physical pain and higher levels of depression than participants without the condition. However, another pattern emerged when Tracy examined their daily routines.

Participants who maintained more consistent schedules tended to report less pain and fewer depressive symptoms, regardless of their sleep quality. This suggests that keeping regular daily habits may be associated with better health even when sleep problems persist.

"Regardless of sleep quality, those who reported having a regular daily routine had lower levels of physical pain and less depression compared to those without a daily routine," Tracy said. "If we are consistent with when we wake up, eat, work or study, interact with others and go to bed, those time cues help synchronize our internal body clocks. Over the long term, that seems to be linked with improved health outcomes."

One possible explanation involves the circadian rhythm, the body's natural 24-hour timing system. This internal clock helps coordinate when we feel awake or sleepy and influences numerous biological processes, including hormone activity, metabolism, and mood.

Rather than operating independently of our surroundings, the circadian system responds to signals that help it keep time. Light and darkness are especially important, but regular activities such as eating, working, interacting with others, and sleeping can also provide timing cues.

When these signals follow a predictable pattern, they help keep the body's biological rhythms aligned. Irregular schedules, on the other hand, can interfere with that coordination.

"When we regulate our circadian rhythm well, our bodies function well, but if it gets too distracted, our bodies don't function as well," Tracy said.

Although the study did not establish that regular routines directly reduce pain or depression, the findings point to circadian regulation as one possible explanation for the connection.

Even relatively small changes in daily schedules may disrupt the body's internal clock. One common example is social jet lag, which occurs when a person's sleep schedule shifts between workdays and days off.

Someone who wakes up early throughout the week but stays up late and sleeps in on weekends may experience this mismatch. The resulting disruption resembles some of the effects of traveling across time zones, even though the person has never left home.

Tracy suggests that maintaining reasonably consistent schedules throughout the entire week, including weekends, may help limit these disruptions and support healthier circadian rhythms.

"As someone who wakes up and goes to bed at the same time every day, I think a daily routine can be helpful for people of all ages across their lifespan," Tracy said. "There is growing awareness about the concept of social jet lag -- waking up and going to bed at different times on weekends compared to weekdays -- and the disruptions it causes to our circadian rhythm, so hopefully this research helps more people consider the health benefits of a daily routine. Since one-third of our lives will be spent sleeping, I think health and well-being research should be looked at holistically from a 24-hour perspective and not just focus on when we are awake."

A Simple Habit With Potential Health Benefits

The research highlights an aspect of healthy living that can be easy to overlook. While getting enough quality sleep remains important, the consistency of activities throughout the day may also be connected to how people feel physically and emotionally.

Because the study relied on survey data from a relatively small group of older adults, it cannot prove that adopting a regular routine will relieve pain or depression. Larger studies would be needed to establish whether changing daily schedules directly improves these outcomes.

Still, the findings suggest that a predictable daily routine may be a useful component of a broader approach to health, particularly for people experiencing insomnia.

For older adults and potentially people of other ages, simple habits such as maintaining regular waking times, eating meals on a consistent schedule, and limiting major changes in weekend sleep patterns may help support the body's natural rhythms.

The study, "Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults," was published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine.

Materials provided by University of Missouri-Columbia. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials.

They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster. The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA.

It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.

The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute.

"The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," SETI wrote of the broadcast in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's."

The message was designed by astronomy professor Frank Drake of Cornell University (who also developed the famed Drake Equation for alien life), as well as Cornnell graduate students Richard Isaacman and Linda May, and Arecibo staff member James Walker, with input from astronomer Carl Sagan and others, according to Cornell University.

The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers, with the broadcast lasting less than 3 minutes, according to SETI.

As of 2026, the message should have traveled about 52 light-years (1 light-year is the distance light travels in a year), with 24,948 light-years to go before reaching star cluster M13.

The Arecibo message may have been the first message of its kind, but it wasn't the last. We have also included messages on several spacecraft, such as Pioneer and Voyager. NASA and Paul McCartney also beamed a performance of "Across the Universe" in 2008.

#698. Archie Renaux on ‘War’s Resident — and Misunderstood — Bad Boy

"He's done some mad things," says the breakout star of George Kay's HBO divorce drama. "But he's in a state of constant stress and people do weird stuff when they're in shock."

Archie Renaux is hesitant to call his character in War a villain. Johnny, the ambitious (often to a fault) junior lawyer who plays a double-agent litigator in the slick divorce drama, is often the one called upon to do the dirty work: the double-crossing, the manipulating of both witnesses and plaintiffs, and then, of course, the whole business of being a mole. “He does awful things, but he’s a puppet more so than anything else,” says Renaux. “He’s been taken advantage of, really.”

The series, from George Kay (Lupin), follows two rival London firms — the white-shoe Cathcarts and the newer, scrappier Taylor & Byrne — as they represent a tech mogul (played by Dominic West) and an actress (Sienna Miller) at the tumultuous end of their marriage. Renaux’s Johnny ostensibly works for Taylor & Byrne, but has been promised an eventual job at Cathcarts in exchange for double-crossing information about the high-profile case. Throughout the season, we see him cheating on his girlfriend with Miller’s Carla and framing a fellow junior lawyer after he’s almost caught with compromising inside intel. The actor, who previously starred on Netflix’s Shadow and Bone, likens the behavior to what happens in the third act of The Drama. Related Stories TV 'The Gilded Age' Scores Season 5 Renewal at HBO Movies Parker Posey Knows Career Highs and Lows. Right Now, She's Having a Blast

“There’s that great bit where Robert Pattinson has a kiss with someone, and it comes out of nowhere,” he explains. “And it’s like, what are you doing mate? Why are you making these decisions? But he’s just manic, and I was watching it in the cinema going, oh, that’s what Johnny’s like. He’s manic.”

In the series finale, Johnny redeems himself — at least as far as his interference with the court case is concerned, but his personal life is seemingly left in shambles. Below, Renaux talks about his take on the episode, what he knows about the show’s pending second season, and what it was like to act alongside Sienna Miller.

What do you remember about the audition process for the show?

I was on another job and we were doing night shoots in Canada, and I got an email about the audition but it was so hectic that I didn’t feel like I could afford to give my attention to anything else. This happened on Shadow and Bone, too, where my agents really pushed me to audition because they said it was really good. They were like, you’ve got to read this. The audition scene was when Johnny’s getting interviewed by Cathcarts, so it was a lengthy paragraph of dialogue I had to learn. And I had an offer for another show at the time, and I couldn’t keep that project waiting too long if I wasn’t going to take it, so I got the offer for War very quickly.

How did you make the decision that you wanted to hold out for the role in War and not the other offer?

It was the character. Johnny’s the audience’s way in. You’re really rooting for him at the beginning, or at least I hope so, and then people are quite disappointed by what he does. But that’s great. It’s complex and divisive. When I was reading the script, I was going, oh God, why’s he done this and that?

Everyone on this show is badly behaved to a degree, but he’s often the person that you feel like could be making better choices…

The other people are smooth-talking, very well put-together, calculated villains. The typical sort. Johnny is not that. He’s done some mad things, the cheating, and he’s a mess. But he’s in a state of constant stress and people do weird stuff when they’re in shock.

Some of what he does feels calculated — but calculated incorrectly — but do you think his affair with Carla was planned or did he get swept up in her beauty and fame?

The way I saw it at the start was, OK, he’s playing the game. If he gets close to the client, and the client’s able to give him information, that’s great. Obviously he’s attracted to her, and he plays along and flirts, and then he enjoys the flirting. When it’s reciprocated, I think it takes him by surprise and he gets caught up in the moment.

Where do you think the desperation comes from?

I wonder if he would have done any of it had he not got fired. Or had Angus not provoked him at the restaurant at the beginning and made him feel insecure about his job. That ignites a sense of, I’m going to succeed by any means necessary. Being around people that have money and big careers is very humiliating, and I think that restaurant scene is something of a villain origin story. I know he does punch him, but I imagine everyone thinks, OK, that’s fair.

In the final episode, when he convinces Flora to come take the stand and to read the letter to Carla, is that him being sneaky again to try and win the case to get himself out of a jam? Or is he trying to redeem himself on a deeper level?

I think it was trying to fix the mess he’d made. I think he’s a good person. I know he is. He knows that’s the least he could have done. He lost everything trying to get what he wanted and going about it in the wrong way. He’s got some sneaky skills and this is him putting them to good use. I think he is a good lawyer, and you only get a glimpse of that. His real personality is when he’s working at the restaurant at the beginning of the season. When he’s interviewing at the law firms, it’s a performance he’s putting on and he’s overcompensating for his education and background.

What did they tell you about plans for future seasons of the show?

Well they’ve got plans for multiple seasons, and it’s sort of an anthology series following the two law firms over different cases. So I knew there was a possibility for doing more seasons. I don’t want to say much more right now.
